A. 
Consultants 
13 
Q. 
Please describe the SRRP’s adjustments to consultants expense. 
14 
A. 
The SRRP (at 9, 13) proposes to disallow $0.364 million and $0.076 million 
15 
for electric and gas, respectively, in costs associated with work performed by 
16 
a consultant, AlixPartners LLP, in the Historic Test Year.  The basis for the 
17 
adjustment is the SRRP’s belief that these charges will not recur in the Rate 
18 
Year (at 11-13).   
19 
 
20 


--- Page 9 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 7 of 120 
 
Q. 
Does the Company agree with Staff’s proposed disallowance? 
1 
A. 
No.  As explained in the responses to IRs DPS-723, set forth in Exhibit __ 
2 
(RRP-5R), and DPS-954, set forth in Exhibit __ (SRRP-3), the Company uses 
3 
consultants like AlixPartners LLP to provide services aimed at proactively 
4 
looking for ways to maintain existing efficiencies; ensuring the effective 
5 
operation of the IT portfolio; staying abreast of cyber security concerns; and 
6 
continually looking for ways to improve overall IT performance.  While the 
7 
SRRP contends that “the engagement with AlixPartners LLC was completed 
8 
in March 2019 and therefore these costs are not expected to reoccur in the 
9 
Rate Year” (at 11), the Company contends that it will continue to engage the 
10 
services of consultants like AlixPartners LLP to look proactively for ways to 
11 
maintain existing efficiencies and ensure the effective operation of the 
12 
portfolio.  Such work would be expected of any major company with an IT 
13 
portfolio as large as the Company’s – especially given the potential benefits 
14 
that could accrue to customers from this work.  The Company submits that it 
15 
would be unreasonable and imprudent if it did not use a consultant to perform 
16 
this type of work again in the Rate Year.  The IT portfolio is ever-changing to 
17 
keep up with evolving customer and stakeholder needs.  As explained in the 
18 
response to IR DPS-954, the Historic Test Year costs for AlixPartners LLP act 
19 
as a proxy for the costs to perform this type of work, which will recur in the 
20 


--- Page 10 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 8 of 120 
 
Rate Year and Data Years.  Therefore, these costs are fully expected to recur 
1 
in the Rate Year and should not be adjusted from the cost of service. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
The SRRP also contends (at 12) that the firm was selected because it is a 
4 
“niche consultancy firm” and “would be able to assist in determining an 
5 
IS transformation plan” so the costs will not recur in the Rate Year.  Does 
6 
the Company agree with the SRRP’s position?  
7 
A. 
No.  The SRRP’s view of the work that AlixPartners LLP was engaged to 
8 
perform and what constitutes recurring work is too narrowly focused for two 
9 
reasons.  First, as noted above, the work performed by AlixPartners LLP is 
10 
significantly more expansive than suggested in the SRRP’s testimony and 
11 
includes (i) identifying IT efficiency opportunities; (ii) benchmarking and 
12 
identifying best practices of other IT organizations,; (iii) analyzing system 
13 
investment opportunities; (iv) assisting with contract negotiations to improve 
14 
vendor spend; and (v) identifying and assessing cyber security and compliance 
15 
risks.  This work will continue in the Rate Year, whether it is performed by 
16 
AlixPartners LLP or a different IT consultant.  Second, work performed by 
17 
AlixPartners LLP is but one item under a broad category of work that is 
18 
performed to manage the IT portfolio.  Although this specific item may not 
19 
recur every year, that does not mean that other work to evaluate and assess the 
20 
IT portfolio will not recur.  For instance, work to assist with contract 
21 


--- Page 11 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 9 of 120 
 
negotiations, work to analyze system investments, and benchmarking with 
1 
other organizations is all work that consultants such as AlixPartners LLP 
2 
provide and will continue to provide in the Rate Year.  Similarly, Company’s 
3 
recent management audit included a recommendation that the Company 
4 
develop IT performance metrics; AlixPartners LLP or a similar consultant will 
5 
likely be engaged to perform this work.    
6 
 
7 
Q. 
Are there additional reasons why the SRRP’s adjustment should be 
8 
rejected? 
9 
A. 
Yes.  As explained in the response to IR DPS-723 and DPS-948, the work 
10 
performed by AlixPartners LLP resulted in Historic Test Year run rate savings 
11 
of $6.8 million, of which $7.019 million in savings is reflected in the revenue 
12 
requirement for the Rate Year.  Therefore, customers received a significant 
13 
benefit from the very work for which the SRRP seeks to disallow cost 
14 
recovery. This further shows the unreasonableness of the SRRP’s proposed 
15 
adjustment.

B. 
Contractors 
7 
Q. 
Please describe the SRRP’s adjustment (at 14-15) to contractors expense. 
8 
A. 
The SRRP recommends (at 14-15) a reduction to contractor expense related to 
9 
the New York State Department of Transportation (“NYSDOT”) Route 5S 
10 
Utica Project (“Utica Project”), which involved the relocation of underground 
11 
electric assets to allow the NYSDOT to reconfigure a state road.  The SRRP 
12 
argues that the costs for the Utica Project “are an anomaly and significantly 
13 
exceed the Contractors expenses typically incurred by the Company on similar 
14 
mandatory NYSDOT projects undertaken in the past three years.”  Although 
15 
the SRRP agrees (at 17) that the Company will incur operating costs to 
16 
relocate assets to accommodate NYSDOT projects, Staff argues that the Utica 
17 
Project should be excluded from the contractor expense forecast because the 
18 
Utica Project is complete and similar relocation projects will not occur at the 
19 
same magnitude as the Company incurred in the Historic Test Year.  After 
20 


--- Page 13 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 11 of 120 
 
adjusting for inflation, the SRRP’s adjustment results in a reduction of $3.597 
1 
million to the Company’s electric contractor expense. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Does the Company agree with the SRRP’s adjustment? 
4 
A. 
No.  The SRRP’s adjustment takes too narrow a view of the Company’s 
5 
contractor expense.  In the normal course of business, the Company incurs 
6 
electric distribution operating expenses (“OpEx”) associated with capital 
7 
expenditures (“CapEx”), which includes contractor expense, at a historic ratio 
8 
of approximately ten percent based on the most recent three-year average.  
9 
Although the Company is not currently aware of any specific NYSDOT 
10 
projects similar in scope to the Utica Project in the Rate Year, these projects 
11 
can arise without significant lead time and the scope can be significant.  
12 
Separately, and more importantly, the aggregate distribution investment 
13 
ultimately agreed to by Staff will be comprised, in total, of projects that 
14 
require approximately ten percent ratio for OpEx associated with CapEx 
15 
independent of any single project.   
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Please explain how the Company forecasts OpEx associated with CapEx 
18 
as well as incremental OpEx associated with CapEx? 
19 
A. 
Generally, the Company inflates OpEx associated with CapEx embedded in 
20 
its historic test year.  Additionally, the Company uses a three-year average for 
21 


--- Page 14 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 12 of 120 
 
forecasting incremental OpEx associated with CapEx based on an accepted 
1 
Commission-approved methodology in Case 10-E-0050, Case 12-E-0201, and 
2 
Case 17-E-0238 as reflected in Exhibit__(RRP-11CU), Workpapers to 
3 
Exhibit___(RRP-3CU), Schedule 27, Workpaper 1.  In Case 10-E-0050, Staff 
4 
modified the methodology to apply the three-year average to the historic test 
5 
year for an historic test year normalization adjustment.  The Commission did 
6 
not make an adjustment to these costs in its “Order Setting Rates” in that 
7 
proceeding.  The Commission also adopted the terms of the Joint Proposals in 
8 
Cases 12-E-0201 and 12-G-0202 (the “2012 Rate Case”) and the 2017 Rate 
9 
Case in which the three-year average methodology was utilized.  The use of 
10 
the three-year average acknowledges that there will be projects that have 
11 
higher OpEx associated with CapEx percentages than the three-year average 
12 
that will offset projects with lower percentages, but overall the historic 
13 
percentages will continue into the Rate Year.   
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Is it appropriate to remove a single project from the Company’s Historic 
16 
Test Year for purposes of forecasting Rate Year costs? 
17 
A. 
No, for two reasons.  First, the three-year normalization adjustment described 
18 
above already ensures that the three-year average is applied to the Historic 
19 
Test Year and therefore this adjustment ignores that a normalization 
20 
adjustment has already been made.  Second, selectively removing a specific 
21 


--- Page 15 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 13 of 120 
 
NYSDOT project from the Historic Test Year average is inappropriate as it 
1 
does not consider the approved methodology for forecasting incremental 
2 
OpEx associated with CapEx and this defeats the purpose of a multi-year 
3 
average.  In the 2017 Rate Case, the SAP objected to the selective removal – 
4 
or “cherry picking” – of individual projects in calculating the historic OpEx 
5 
related to CapEx ratio.  As the SAP acknowledged in its testimony for that 
6 
case (at 19-20), “multi-year averages are used specifically to address the 
7 
impact of individual projects.  The Company cannot simply remove a handful 
8 
of projects with the result of increasing the average and ignore projects with a 
9 
reciprocal effect.”  The adjustment of the specific NYSDOT project is 
10 
contrary to the SAP’s position in the 2017 Rate Case, as the Company will 
11 
undertake projects with OpEx that exceeds the ten percent average ratio, as 
12 
well as projects that have no OpEx, such as new construction projects. 
13

C. 
Service Company Rent Expense 
15 
Q. 
Does Staff make any adjustments to Service Company rent expense? 
16 
A. 
Yes.  Staff proposes six adjustments to Service Company rent expense:  four 
17 
adjustments are proposed by the SITP and two adjustments are proposed by 
18 
the SAP. 
19 
 
20 


--- Page 16 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 14 of 120 
 
Q. 
Please describe SITP’s first adjustment. 
1 
A. 
The SITP (at 59) recommends an adjustment of $0.890 million for electric and 
2 
$1.799 million for gas to Rate Year Service Company rent expense to reflect 
3 
its reduction of costs related to National Grid’s Gas Business Enablement 
4 
(“GBE”) program.  As discussed in the Panel’s direct testimony (at 51-52), for 
5 
ratemaking purposes, the Company proposes to increase the GBE program 
6 
cost cap from the $458.1 million agreed to in the 2017 Rate Case to $530.9 
7 
million while at the same time recognizing that Niagara Mohawk’s 
8 
proportional allocation of GBE Program costs has decreased because of 
9 
changes in the allocation factor used to allocate those costs among National 
10 
Grid’s affiliates.  The impact of the Company’s proposed adjustment is that 
11 
Niagara Mohawk’s revenue requirement would reflect the same level of GBE 
12 
Program costs as the revenue requirement adopted in the 2017 Rate Case.  The 
13 
SITP recommends that the Company’s proposed adjustment to the GBE cost 
14 
cap be rejected.   
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Does the Company agree with the SITP’s recommendation?   
17 
A. 
No.  The SITP’s recommendation is both unreasonable and illogical.  The 
18 
SITP has lost sight of the fact that the GBE cost cap adopted by the 
19 
Commission in Niagara Mohawk’s 2017 Rate Case was intended solely to 
20 
establish the costs allocated to Niagara Mohawk.  In establishing the GBE 
21 


--- Page 17 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 15 of 120 
 
cost cap, the Commission was not purporting to regulate Service Company or 
1 
to establish the level of GBE costs that could or should be reflected in rates by 
2 
any other Niagara Mohawk affiliate.  This is clearly evidenced by the explicit 
3 
language of Section 7.8.1 of the Joint Proposal adopted by the Commission in 
4 
the 2017 Rate Case.  This provision states: 
5 
For purposes of determining Niagara Mohawk’s allocable 
6 
share of GBE Program costs, the total Service Company costs, 
7 
comprised of capital and project operating expenses related to 
8 
capital expenses, for the GBE Program will be capped at 
9 
$458.1 million through FY 2023.  In future rate proceedings, 
10 
the Company may seek recovery of costs in excess of this cap 
11 
that are associated with incremental investments in the GBE 
12 
Program beyond those described in Appendix 10, Schedule 1 
13 
as long as the incremental costs are justified by measurable 
14 
benefits. 
15 
 
16 
As the quoted language clearly states, the GBE program cost cap was 
17 
established solely for “purposes of determining Niagara Mohawk’s allocable 
18 
share of GBE program costs.”  That “allocable share” was the amount of costs 
19 
that was determined using the allocation factors that were in effect at the time 
20 
rates were established in the 2017 Rate Case as applied to $458.1 million of 
21 
GBE costs.  This “allocable share” was the amount of costs that were reflected 
22 
in the Company’s revenue requirement that was approved by the Commission.  
23 
In proposing to reject the Company’s proposal to update the GBE cost cap to 
24 
permit the Company to recover in rates the same amount of GBE costs as the 
25 
“allocable share” approved by the Commission in the 2017 Rate Case, the 
26 


--- Page 18 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 16 of 120 
 
SITP has offered no meaningful reason why the Company should be required 
1 
to absorb a significant disallowance of GBE costs as compared to the level 
2 
that was previously approved for recovery merely because National Grid’s 
3 
allocation factors have changed. 
4 
 
5 
Q. 
You stated that the SITP’s recommendation is illogical.  Please explain 
6 
why this is the case. 
7

Q. 
In arriving at its IT forecast adjustment, the SITP performed a linear 
11 
regression analysis to measure the historic trend in actual IT spending.  
12 
Has the Panel reviewed the SITP’s linear regression analysis? 
13 
A. 
Yes. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Does the Company agree with the SITP’s approach used to arrive at its 
16 
IT capital forecast? 
17 
A. 
No.  Linear regression is used to determine whether a linear relationship exists 
18 
in a data set such that the relationship can be used to predict future results.  
19 
The data set is comprised of points that measure the relationship between at 
20 
least two variables:  an independent variable, which is expected to be the 
21 


--- Page 22 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 20 of 120 
 
causation variable, and a dependent variable, which is supposed to be the 
1 
effect.  There is no basis for concluding that a linear relationship exists or 
2 
should exist between fiscal years and IT capital investment levels.  Indeed, as 
3 
shown on Exhibit __ (SITP-2), the Company’s proposed IT capital investment 
4 
levels fluctuate up and down year over year depending on the nature of 
5 
projected capital investments planned for a given year.  Therefore, a linear 
6 
regression analysis is simply not an appropriate tool to use to forecast future 
7 
investment levels or to develop appropriate levels of IT investment for 
8 
ratemaking purposes. 
9 
 
10 
Further, for a regression analysis of past performance to be used to predict 
11 
future results, there should be an expectation that future conditions will be 
12 
similar to the past conditions used for the analysis.  Here, however, the 
13 
regression analysis covers a period that does not include spending on projects 
14 
such as the proposed ADMS, Grid Modernization, and VOLT Enablement 
15 
projects and therefore is not representative of the Company’s future IT 
16 
investment expectations for those projects.  Nonetheless, Staff applies the 
17 
result achieved through its forecasting adjustment to reduce the cost of those 
18 
projects.  This was inappropriate.  To the extent that an argument can be made 
19 
that the SITP’s regression based forecasting methodology could be applied at 
20 
all – it should be applied solely to the Company’s Core IT spending. 
21 


--- Page 23 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 21 of 120 
 
Q. 
Does the Panel have any concerns with the results of the SITP’s 
1 
regression analysis? 
2 
A. 
The weakness of the SITP’s regression analysis is demonstrated by the R-
3 
squared value result of the regression equation.  The R-squared value is a 
4 
statistical term that indicates how well the trend line fits to the data.  An R-
5 
squared value of 1.00 indicates a perfect fit.  The R-squared value obtained by 
6 
the SITP, 0.6212 is not robust and should have caused the SITP to abandon its 
7 
regression-based approach. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Has the Company discovered any additional flaws with the linear 
10 
regression analysis produced by the SITP? 
11 
A. 
Yes.  Though the Company firmly believes the linear regression analysis is an 
12 
incorrect tool for determining future spending levels of the IT organization, 
13 
there are additional steps that could have been taken to calculate a more 
14 
accurate R-squared value.  It would have been more appropriate for Staff to 
15 
normalize the spending reflected in 2017 and 2018 by averaging the spend in 
16 
those years.  A significant portion of the 2017 IT capital spend was the result 
17 
of advancing planned investments on projects in National Grid’s Technology 
18 
Improvement Project from 2018 and beyond.  In other words, a significant 
19 
portion of the FY 2017 actual spend had the effect of suppressing actual 
20 
spending in FY 2018 and beyond, a result that Staff’s regression equation 
21 


--- Page 24 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 22 of 120 
 
makes no adjustment for in 2018 and 2019.  Second,  it would have been more 
1 
appropriate for Staff to have extended the data used in the regression analysis 
2 
to include the most recent actual + forecasted spending for FY 2021.  In 
3 
Schedule 4 to Exhibit__(RRP-2R), the Company updated the regression 
4 
analysis to include the normalized average of 2017 and 2018 spending and 
5 
updated the data set to include the forecast FY 2021 spending.  The forecasted 
6 
FY 2021 spending was comprised of the actual spend for the eight-month 
7 
period from March to November and a four-month forecast for December 
8 
through March based on the average monthly spend for the prior eight 
9 
months.  This resulted in an R-squared value of 0.8826 and raised the 
10 
forecasted Rate Year Core IT CapEx to $202.96 million from Staff’s 
11 
calculated spending level of $174.548 million.  For these reasons, the SITP’s 
12 
methodology used to arrive at its IT capital forecast is flawed and therefore 
13 
should be rejected.

I. 
Transportation Expense 
1 
Q. 
The SAP stated (at 31) that the Company’s lease agreements for fleet 
2 
vehicles and equipment are capital leases.  Is this correct?  
3 
A. 
No, this is incorrect.  The Company’s lease agreements are operating leases 
4 
that never transfer title or ownership of the leased assets to the Company.  The 
5 
Company’s lease agreements contain a clause that allows for the continued 
6 
use of a leased asset after it is fully amortized.  Thereafter, the Company pays 
7 
a management fee for this privilege.  The lease vendor continues to pay 
8 
applicable taxes as owner of the assets and passes these ownership costs, in 
9 
addition to the management fees, to the Company through lease invoices.  
10 
Ultimately, when the leased assets are dispositioned, the lease management 
11 
company sells the assets at auction and returns the difference of the auction 
12 
proceeds, auction fees, and any remaining unamortized value (if applicable) to 
13 
the Company as a credit to lease expense. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
How much did the Company spend in net lease expense in the Historic 
16 
Test Year? 
17 
A. 
The Company spent $34.714 million in the Historic Test Year for net lease 
18 
expense as presented in Exhibit __ (RRP-3R), Schedule 24, Page 6.  Net lease 
19 
expense includes lease interest, lease amortization, and credited proceeds from 
20 
sale of surplus assets. 
21 


--- Page 46 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 44 of 120 
 
Q. 
How much did the Company forecast in net lease expense for the Rate 
1 
Year? 
2 
A. 
The Company forecast $42.991 million in net lease expense as presented in 
3 
Exhibit __ (RRP-3R), Schedule 24, Page 6. 
4 
 
5 
Q. 
Please response to the SAP’s statement (at 27) that the Company’s Rate 
6 
Year forecast of $24.371 million for new leases “is 443% greater than the 
7 
amount incurred by the Company over the most recent three-year 
8 
period.” 
9 
A. 
This statement is an unfair comparison and misleading.  As explained in the 
10 
response to DPS-1053, replacement lease costs calculated on a one-year basis, 
11 
as they were in response to DPS-457 for years 2017, 2018, and 2019, are not 
12 
comparable to the $24.371 million Rate Year replacement lease costs 
13 
calculated on a cumulative basis over the 2.5 year period beginning January 
14 
2020 through June 2022.  The total lease costs for 2017, 2018, and 2019, 
15 
calculated on a one-year basis will reflect less than twelve months of lease 
16 
costs in each of those years depending on the month in which the vehicles 
17 
were replaced in that year.  Simply adding the replacement vehicle lease costs 
18 
for these three years on an individual basis will not yield the same result as 
19 
adding vehicle replacement lease costs on a cumulative basis over a three-year 
20 
period.  In the latter case, the vehicle replacement lease costs would include a 
21 


--- Page 47 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 45 of 120 
 
full twelve months of lease costs for all 2017 and 2018 replacement leases by 
1 
2019. 
2 
 
3 
In addition, the SAP’s comparison of spending in the Rate Year (due to the 
4 
replacement of existing vehicles between January 2020 through June 2022) to 
5 
the spending from CY 2017 to CY 2019 shown in the response to IR DPS-457 
6 
is misleading.  As an initial matter, the SAP (at 27) appears to have 
7 
miscalculated the total spend from CY 2017 to CY 2019 shown in the 
8 
response to DPS-457, which is $4.847 million, rather than $4.485 million 
9 
stated by the SAP.  Even with this correction, the comparison between the 
10 
Rate Year and CY 2017 to CY 2019 is still misleading because it is not an 
11 
indication of the magnitude of cost increase for new leases.  Rather, this 
12 
merely indicates that there are a greater number of vehicles that the Company 
13 
must replace from January 2020 to the Rate Year than there were in the three-
14 
year period from 2017 to 2019.  The increase in costs due to new leases for 
15 
replacement is driven directly by the number of replacements, which is, in 
16 
turn, driven by the ages of the underlying assets.  As existing vehicles reach 
17 
ages beyond original lease terms, this results in a decrease to forecast lease 
18 
expense for those pre-existing leases.  Therefore, Staff’s issue is with the 
19 
number of vehicles being replaced, not the actual cost to replace these 
20 
vehicles.  Staff exaggerates this point by focusing on the increase in new lease 
21 


--- Page 48 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 46 of 120 
 
expense, rather than the number of vehicles replaced, and comparing a small 
1 
subset of the Company’s fleet (the vehicles replaced from 2017-2019) to a 
2 
much larger subset of the Company’s fleet (the number of vehicles replaced 
3 
from January 2020 through the Rate Year).  Also, the increase in replacement 
4 
volume leads to an increase in forecast auction proceeds at sale, which are 
5 
credited back to the Company’s lease expense.  Finally, Staff’s focus on new 
6 
lease expense also exaggerates the increase by ignoring the cost of all vehicles 
7 
in the Company’s fleet that are not being replaced between January 2020 and 
8 
the Rate Year.  When considering all factors, including the number of 
9 
vehicles, auction proceeds, and non-replacement vehicles, the Company’s 
10 
Rate Year adjustment to the Historic Test Year is therefore $8.277 million.

P. 
Savings 
11 
Q. 
What level of savings is typically reflected in a rate filing? 
12 
A. 
Rate cases traditionally include a productivity adjustment on the premise that 
13 
well-run companies should be able to find a modest measure of efficiencies 
14 
in the rate year.  The adjustment is typically calculated as one percent of total 
15 
labor expense and payroll taxes in recognition of how difficult it is to 
16 
achieve savings year after year.  In this case, the traditional productivity 
17 
adjustment would result in Rate Year savings totaling $9.152 million across 
18 
the electric and gas business.  The Company, however, went above and 
19 
beyond the Commission’s traditional efficiency standard, reflecting Rate 
20 
Year cost reductions of more than $48 million.  The scale and scope of these 
21 


--- Page 81 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 79 of 120 
 
savings is more than five times the level typically reflected in a rate filing, 
1 
demonstrating the magnitude of the Company’s efforts.   
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Will this level of savings be difficult to achieve? 
4 
A. 
Yes.  It is a challenge for any business to achieve a one percent efficiency 
5 
reduction each year let alone five times that number.  To reduce costs of this 
6 
magnitude requires significant effort, and the pandemic has challenged, and 
7 
will continue to challenge, the Company’s ability to deliver on this 
8 
aspirational effort.  For example, the field excellence program involves the 
9 
use of real-time performance boards and coaching in the field to help 
10 
advance Accelerate Program initiatives.  This work is not possible, however, 
11 
in the current environment where office staff have been largely working 
12 
from home.  Moreover, should a second wave of the pandemic result, it is 
13 
likely that non-essential work could again be paused, further impacting the 
14 
Accelerate Program. 
15 
 
16 
 
Notwithstanding these challenges, the Company reflected the full forecast of 
17 
reasonably achievable Accelerate Program savings in the Rate Year (i.e., 
18 
savings from initiatives in implementation levels (“ILs”) 4 and 5).  On top of 
19 
this, while the Company would have been within its right to not reflect a 
20 
productivity adjustment given the presence of the Accelerate Program, the 
21

or 5 in the Rate Year.

implemented in the Historic Test Year.  They have not moved to IL 4 yet 
8 
because, to move from IL 3 to IL 4, the initiative must demonstrate the 
9 
ability to evidence savings.  This is done by quantifying and tracking savings 
10 
as compared to actual costs over a period of successive months.  To date, 
11 
these six initiatives have been unable to demonstrate savings.  If they do, 
12 
because they were implemented in the Historic Test Year, any savings are 
13 
therefore already reflected in the revenue requirements through lower 
14 
Historic Test Year costs.  Table 3 below shows (i) the ten initiatives for 
15

16

17

18 
the revenue requirement if the Commission were to agree with the SRRP’s

B. 
Income Tax Repair Deduction Customer Benefit 
10 
Q. 
The SAP (at 75) states that the Company has not adequately supported 
11 
its proposal to establish a deferral mechanism to recover interest 
12 
expenses related to the income tax audit.  Is the Company providing 
13 
additional documentation to prove that customers received the benefit of 
14 
the repair deduction to support the request for deferral of interest paid as 
15 
a result of the IRS audit of fiscal years 2010-2012? 
16 
A. 
Yes, the Company is providing additional documentation.  Exhibit __ (RRP-
17 
4R), Schedule 1, provides a timeline of the significant and relevant events 
18 
related to the original change in tax accounting that gave rise to a large repair 
19 
deduction in the fiscal year ending March 31, 2009, through the eventual 
20 
disallowance of a portion of that deduction.  Exhibit __ (RRP-4) also 
21 


--- Page 108 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 106 of 120 
 
illustrates the impact of the repair deduction to customers’ rates.  The original 
1 
deduction gave rise to a deferred tax liability, which reduces rate base, thus 
2 
giving customers the benefit of the cash refund received by the Company for 
3 
the reduction in taxable income.  That reduction in rates occurs when the rates 
4 
become effective in a rate case in which the deferred tax liability is included 
5 
in rate base.  The Company did not file a full rate case including the tax 
6 
impact of the deduction until the 2012 Rate Case.  In Case 10-E-0050 the 
7 
Company was required to establish a regulatory liability to return to customers 
8 
the cash flow benefit of the repair deduction, but the calculation basis for the 
9 
liability was the cash refund amount, not the deferred tax liability arising from 
10 
the change in repair accounting.  The reason for the cash refund for tax year 
11 
2009 was change in accounting method to recognize repairs as a current 
12 
expense for tax purposes.  The Company is not calculating any customer 
13 
benefit for this time period in this case, although clearly a significant benefit 
14 
was provided to customers.  Any benefit calculated would be in addition to the 
15 
approximate $25 million of benefits already quantified in the customer benefit 
16 
calculation.  The forecast period for the 2012 Rate Case included a deferred 
17 
tax rate base adjustment.  The 2017 Rate Case reset the deferred tax liability 
18 
to the tax return position, so customers once again benefitted from the full 
19 
repair deduction and have continued and will continue to do so until new rates 
20 
from this rate filing become effective. 
21 


--- Page 109 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 107 of 120 
 
 
The calculation of the repair tax deduction benefit received by customers as a 
1 
result of the 2012 Rate Case and the 2017 Rate Case is set forth on Exhibit __ 
2 
(RRP-4R), Schedules 4 through 7 and Schedules 8 through 13, which cover 
3 
the periods the Company is claiming the customers received a benefit of the 
4 
full repair deduction.  There are two components to the 2009 repair deduction:  
5 
the full deduction and the subsequent tax reserve (hereafter referred to and 
6 
included in documentation as FIN 48, which provided accounting guidance 
7 
related to uncertain income tax positions) for what eventually becomes an 
8 
audit disallowance of a portion of that deduction.  For customers to receive the 
9 
benefit of the deduction in rates that gave rise to the interest payment that the 
10 
Company is requesting recovery for, the full deferred tax liability, not 
11 
including the FIN 48 reserve, must have been included in rate base.  
12 
Schedules 4 through 7 provide analysis and support for the balance of deferred 
13 
tax in the 2012 Rate Case, and Schedules 8 through 13 provide the same 
14 
analysis and support for the deferred tax balance in the 2017 Rate Case.  The 
15 
calculation of rate base deferred tax balances in the subsequent rate and data 
16 
years is a result of taking the historic test year balance and adding the plant 
17 
related activity in the rate and data years.  The calculation of all movement in 
18 
the deferred tax balances from the starting point of the historic test year is 
19 
documented in the exhibits and schedules provided in each rate case.  Thus, 
20 
because the beginning balance includes the full repair deduction, the 
21 


--- Page 110 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 108 of 120 
 
subsequent rate years do as well, unless a specific adjustment to remove the 
1 
deduction was effectuated – which did not occur. 
2 
 
 
3 
 
Schedules 4 through 13 provide the analysis of and the support for the historic 
4 
test year end deferred tax balance.  The schedule begins with the deferred tax 
5 
general ledger balance, adds an adjustment for the tax regulatory accounts 
6 
(FAS 109), and then includes adjustments for the deferred tax related to the 
7 
underlying pre-tax accounts that are not in rate base, all totaling to the final 
8 
rate base amount.  The FIN 48 balance for the repair reserve is generally 
9 
reversed out.  It is important to note that, for regulatory purposes, FIN 48 
10 
reserve accounting for temporary differences needs to be reversed.  The effect 
11 
of this reversal is to present rate base deferred taxes that match up to filed tax 
12 
returns that have affected the Company’s cash flow, rather than a hypothetical 
13 
position that the Company believes may occur after the completion of an 
14 
income tax audit.  During the period including the historic test year for the 
15 
2012 Rate Case, the ledger was maintained on a FERC accounting basis, 
16 
which matches up to the regulatory accounting method.  Thus, the FIN 48 
17 
reserves for the repair audit adjustment were not included and customers 
18 
received the full benefit of the repair deduction.  At the time of the historic 
19 
test year for the 2017 Rate Case, the Company had switched to maintaining its 
20 
ledger on a US GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) basis, 
21 


--- Page 111 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 109 of 120 
 
including the deferred tax impacts of FIN 48 reserve.  For regulatory rate base 
1 
purposes, FIN 48 reserve reflected on the US GAAP books must be reversed 
2 
and that reversal is included in the rate case adjustment column in the historic 
3 
test year schedule as set forth on Exhibit __ (RRP-4R), Schedules 12 and 13. 
4 
 
 
5 
 
The Company has calculated the customer benefit of the various periods that 
6 
the repair related deferred tax balance was included as a reduction to rate base 
7 
and maintains that the customer benefit more than offsets the interest expense 
8 
paid to the IRS and to New York State as a result of the repair deduction 
9 
disallowance.

C. 
Deferral Balances 
7 
Q. 
Please describe the SPP’s position regarding the deferral accounts that 
8 
the Company lists as available for use as a rate mitigator. 
9 
A. 
The SPP did not reflect any of the Company’s available deferral credits in its 
10 
proposed electric and gas base rate decreases.  The SPP states (at 16), 
11 
however, that, if the Commission does not adopt the electric and gas base rate 
12 
decreases recommended by Staff, Staff “would support using a portion of [the 
13 
available] deferral credits to negate or mitigate any increases in revenue 
14 
requirement.”  The SPP further recommends (at 16-17) that, if deferral credits 
15 
are used to offset revenue requirements, “they should be passed back as a 
16 
surcredit, so that base delivery rates reflect the actual cost of service.” 
17 
 
18 
Q. 
Does the Company agree with the use of deferral credits as a rate 
19 
mitigator? 
20 


--- Page 113 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 111 of 120 
 
A. 
Although the Company is not opposed in principle to using a portion of 
1 
existing deferral balances to mitigate rate impacts, the Company believes such 
2 
balances would be most effective and would provide the greatest benefit to 
3 
customers as part of a multi-year settlement.  The Company believes a balance 
4 
must be struck between the appropriate level of regulatory liabilities to use in 
5 
current and future rate mitigation efforts.  Using too large a portion of the 
6 
deferral balances in a one-year period causes significant rate volatility for 
7 
customers, as customers would be subject to significant future rate increases 
8 
when the deferral balance is depleted.  Spreading the deferral balances over 
9 
the course of a multi-year rate plan would allow the Company to smooth out 
10 
the impacts of the deferral credits on rates and better serve both current and 
11 
future customers. 
12

Other Adjustments and Corrections 
13 
 
A. 
TRA Revision 
14 
Q.  
Please describe the Public Policy Transmission Needs (“PPTN”) projects 
15 
that the Company in proposing as part of the New York Independent 
16 
System Operation’s (“NYISO”) Order No. 1000 process. 
17 
A. 
The Company’s capital forecast includes certain upgrades required as part of 
18 
Segment A of the AC Transmission Order No. 1000 PPTN and Western NY 
19 
(“WNY”) Order 1000 PPTN. Specifically, for Segment A the Company’s 
20 
scope of work includes Edic Substation upgrades and reconductoring a portion 
21 


--- Page 117 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 115 of 120 
 
of the Company’s existing Line 30.  The Segment A upgrades were originally 
1 
included in LS Power- NYPA’s capital costs for Segment A.  After discussion 
2 
among the parties however, LS Power – NYPA and the Company agreed that 
3 
the Company would undertake the capital investment for these two upgrades 
4 
proposed in the scope of work for the Segment A Project.  
5 
 
6 
On October 13, 2016, the Commission issued an Order in Case 14-E-0454 and 
7 
recommended that certain transmission issues be addressed by the Company. 
8 
Specifically, the Commission agreed with the NYISO that the Company 
9 
should reconductor its Niagara-Packard 115 kV #193 and #194 lines. 
10 
 
11 
These four NYISO Order No. 1000 PPTN projects have been added to the 
12 
Company’s capital forecast and costs will be allocated to statewide customers 
13 
in accordance with the NYISO Tariffs approved by the Federal Energy 
14 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC”).    
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Please address the SEGRP’s statement (at 56) that they “were not able to 
17 
determine if the costs of these [NYISO Order No. 1000] projects are or 
18 
will be included in the Company’s rate base.  If the costs of these projects 
19 
are included in rate base, it is not appropriate for the Company to retain 
20 


--- Page 118 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 116 of 120 
 
the FERC ROE as proposed by the Company, since ratepayers are 
1 
funding the projects.” 
2 
A.   
Staff appears to be suggesting that if these NYISO Order No. 1000 PPTN 
3 
projects are included in the Company’s rate base, and if the Company’s retail 
4 
customers are paying all the project costs, then the Company should not retain 
5 
the FERC ROE.  This is, however, not the case with these projects.  These 
6 
NYISO Order No. 1000 PPTN projects are being built for regional 
7 
transmission service and the Company supports the NYISO cost allocation 
8 
process under which it would be inappropriate to have the Company’s retail 
9 
customers pay for all the projects’ revenue requirement.  The customers 
10 
paying for these NYISO Order No. 1000 PPTN projects are statewide load, 
11 
not the Company’s retail customers.  Moreover, the recovery of transmission 
12 
rates for these projects is allocated by the NYISO to statewide loads based on 
13 
beneficiary pay principles that are outlined in the NYISO tariffs. 
14 
 
15 
Q. 
Do you agree with SEGRP’s suggestion (at pp. 56-57), that “it is not 
16 
appropriate for the Company to retain the FERC ROE” with respect to 
17 
Order No. 1000 transmission revenues that are to be allocated region-
18 
wide for portions of the PPTN projects?   
19 
A. 
No, the Company believes that the SERGP’s suggestion is incorrect in this 
20 
scenario.  FERC sets the ROE for transmission projects undertaken pursuant 
21 


--- Page 119 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 117 of 120 
 
to Order No. 1000, such as the PPTN projects.  We do not believe there is any 
1 
basis for a different approach here.  Furthermore, the NYISO Open Access 
2 
Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) mechanism governing cost recovery for PPTN 
3 
projects – the Western New York Facilities Charge (“WNY-FC”) (which 
4 
includes provision for “return on investment” (sec. 16.17.2)) – is set forth in a 
5 
separate Schedule of the OATT and is clearly intended to be implemented 
6 
separately from other cost recovery mechanisms.  Thus, Schedule 17 provides 
7 
that the “WNY-FC shall be calculated in accordance with the formula set forth 
8 
in Section 6.17.3” rather than any non-Order 1000 mechanism (sec. 6.17.2), 
9 
and that “[t]he ISO will calculate and bill the WNY-FC separately . . . in 
10 
accordance with this Section” (sec. 6.17.3.1).  Therefore, the Commission’s 
11 
practice for retail rate setting in the context of retail cost recovery should not 
12 
apply to the NYISO Order 1000 projects developed by the Company.  
13 
 
14 
Indeed, as the Company explained in previous testimony, if the Commission 
15 
were to use the revenues paid by jurisdictional loads/customers in other parts 
16 
of the state to reduce the payment to the Company’s retail customers the 
17 
Commission would be creating rate inequity between participating customers; 
18 
negating the beneficiaries pay principles established by the NYISO.  From the 
19 
Company’s perspective, treating the Company differently from other project 
20 
developers competing in the NYISO Order No. 1000 process would be a 
21 


--- Page 120 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
 
Page 118 of 120 
 
significant concern of all the New York utilities and should be rejected in this 
1 
case. 
2

Customer Benefit
Measurement
1
December 2009
National Grid files its consolidated federal income tax return
and combined New York return with a change in accounting
method for a repair deduction. Niagara Mohawk has a
cumulative repair deduction of $842 million.
Customer does not receive benefit at this time
as the Company is between filing of rate cases
and ADIT is not yet reset.
0
2
December 2009
As the provision did not include a repair deduction, the federal
and state return to provision journal entries record the effect in
the ledger. Repair deduction results in a deferred tax liability
recorded to the 282 account.
Schedule 2 - Federal return to provision calculations
Customer does not receive benefit at this time
as the Company is between filing of rate cases
and ADIT is not yet reset.
0
Schedule 3 - State return to provision calculations
3
May 2010
Significant adjustments to the repair study and cumulative
adjustment are calculated by PwC in a revised study. A tax
reserve for the tax effect of the $139.8 expected audit
adjustment is recorded with a current payable of 58.9 million
and deferred tax asset of 58.9 million.
Customer does not receive benefit at this time
as the Company is between filing of rate cases
and ADIT is not yet reset.
0
4
January 2011
NYPSC examined the repair change in methodology during
discovery in case 10-E-0050 and quantified the benefits received
by the Company due to the repair deduction. Result in rate
order is a regulatory liability set up to return the benefits to
customers based on the date that the Company received a cash
refund for the fiscal year 2009 tax return. At that time, it was
recognized that the error would result in an eventual payback
of the benefit to the federal and state governments, so the
known adjustment is not included in the regulatory liability.
See Rate Order Case 10-E-0050 establishing a regulatory
liability of $28.89 million. This number is based on a cash
receipt by Niagara Mohawk of $266.9 million for federal
purposes instead of the benefit generated by the repair
deduction alone.
Customers did receive a benefit for the repair
deduction through the regulatory liability
ordered in case 10-E-0050. The Company is not
quantifying the amount relative to the repair
deferred tax liability for this exercise because
the basis of measurement was a cash refund,
not deferred tax based, although the cash
refund was caused by the repair deduction. Any
additional benefit would be additive to the $25
million total presented here.
0
5
April 2012
Company files rate cases 12-E-0201 and 12-G-0202 with starting
ADIT balance based on historic test year end December 2011,
rates to go into effect April 1, 2013. As starting point is actual
ADIT balance per ledger, the DTL for the full repair deduction is
included.
Schedules 4-7 - Ledger balances and support for ADIT balance
as of March 31, 2012, included as starting point for rate case.
Customers receive benefit of full repair
deduction, including the error beginning April 1,
2013 when rates from this case go into effect.
2,614,615
6
October 2013
Adjustment included in rate case forecast period to adjust ADIT
balance for expected timing of settling 2009 IRS audit, including
the repair adjustment to increase taxable income.
Information included as Attachment 4 in DPS-1007
The adjustment has removed the repair
deduction tax effect for $37.1 million, so
customers are only getting the benefit on $18.3
million of ADIT of rate base until new rates for
17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239 go into effect April 1,
2018.

FROM: 
DPS Staff, Sarah Keymel

National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel and Policy Panel 
SUBJECT:   Accelerate Program (Savings)
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
On p. 15 of the Direct Testimony of the Policy Panel, the Company states, “the Accelerate 
Program ends in FY21[.]”  On p. 86 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements 
Panel, the Company states, “National Grid is committed to continuously identifying 
opportunities to be more efficient and productive for the benefit of its customers.”   
1.
Explain whether the Company will continue to pursue initiatives under and associated 
with the Accelerate Program beyond the end of FY21 (e.g., brainstorm for new 
initiatives, continue to progress current initiatives in all implementation levels, etc.). 
2.
Explain to what extent National Grid has considered new or other savings or efficiency 
programs when the Accelerate Program ends.  If so, provide all supporting 
documentation. 
3.
Excluding the Accelerate Program, explain what other savings or efficiency programs are 
currently in effect at the Company.  Explain the function of each saving or efficiency 
program, and provide or identify the current results of each program, and any timeline for 
anticipated future results. 
Response:  
1-2. 
Although National Grid will always look for ways to reduce its costs, there is no plan to 
continue the Accelerate Program beyond fiscal year 2021 or undertake another program of 
similar magnitude.  As explained in the direct testimony of the Revenue Requirements 
Panel, the Accelerate Program is a unique, three-year efficiency challenge that National 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 6 of 272


--- Page 241 ---
Form 103  
Grid undertook commencing in fiscal year 2019 to deliver an unprecedented level of 
savings for customers.  Specifically, National Grid set an aspirational target of a 20 percent 
productivity improvement across the US business by fiscal year 2021.  
The Commission typically imputes a one percent productivity adjustment on the premise 
that well-run companies should be able to find a modest level of efficiencies in the rate 
year.  The Accelerate Program went above and beyond the efficiency standard set by the 
Commission, purposely setting an ambitious target to challenge the business to deliver 
maximum customer value.  Although National Grid will not achieve its aspirational targets, 
the Company managed to deliver cost reductions of a scale and scope far exceeding the 
modest level of efficiencies typically imputed by the Commission.  This effort has enabled 
the Company to manage costs during the current challenging economic environment posed 
by the pandemic.  Indeed, the current filing reflects efficiencies equivalent to more than 
four times the normal productivity adjustment.  On top of this, the Company included a 
one percent productivity adjustment.  
Once the Accelerate Program ends in fiscal year 2021, the Company, as part of prudent 
utility operations, will endeavor to find efficiencies to lower costs for customers while 
attempting to sustain any efficiencies achieved to date.  The Company, however, has not 
identified any initiatives aside from those currently included in the Accelerate Program. 
3. 
The purpose of the Accelerate Program was to collect all efficiencies initiatives in a single 
program to attempt to mitigate customers’ costs.  Therefore, outside of the Accelerate 
Program there are currently no savings or efficiency programs in place.

Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall

1.
On page 15 of the Direct Testimony of the Policy Panel, the Company states, “While the 
pandemic will undoubtedly challenge the Company’s ability to deliver these savings, as 
the current focus has been on work necessary to maintain safe and reliable service….”  
Explain, in detail, how the pandemic has challenged, and can be expected to further 
challenge, the Company’s ability to deliver the Accelerate Program’s savings. 
2.
On page 87 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Company 
stated that the Accelerate Program commenced in FY 2019.  Has the Company updated, 
refreshed or changed the Accelerate Program since it was first announced?  Explain. 
Response:  
1. 
The pandemic has challenged, and will continue to challenge, National Grid’s ability to 
deliver the aspirational Accelerate Program savings – especially for the initiatives that have 
not advanced to Implementation Levels 4 or 5.   
New York was ground zero for the COVID-19 pandemic.  On March 7, 2020, Governor 
Cuomo declared a state of emergency that is currently effective through September 7, 2020.  
In the immediate aftermath of the pandemic, the Company paused all but essential work.  
This meant prioritizing the critical tasks necessary to maintain safe and reliable service for 
National Grid’s millions of electric and gas customers in New York State.   As National 
Grid focused on developing new work practices to address restrictions caused by the 
pandemic, the work to implement Accelerate Program initiatives was largely paused with 
no reporting between March 28 and July 24.    
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 8 of 272


--- Page 243 ---
Form 103  
Indeed, the state of emergency required significant adjustments to work practices, with 
National Grid transitioning to a work-from-home model for thousands of its employees.  
The transition also required that National Grid’s Information Technology function, which 
is a core enabler of many Accelerate Program initiatives, focus its time and attention to 
ensuring that technology was in place so that employees could work remotely.   
As National Grid’s field forces have begun to resume non-essential work, work on the 
Accelerate Program has resumed; however, the new ways of working continue to present 
some challenges in advancing efficiency initiatives.  For example, the Field Excellence 
program involves performance boards in National Grid’s field barns and coaching teams 
in the field to advise on how to implement and deliver initiatives.  This is not possible in 
the current environment where office staff are largely working from home (and the 
expectation is that this arrangement will continue for at least the next several months).   
The teams are developing new ways of working as they attempt to deliver initiatives.  
National Grid, however, will remain challenged to deliver initiatives that have not 
progressed to Implementation Levels 4 or 5 because of the pandemic impacts, particularly 
as the backlog of critical operational work, which had been paused, is addressed.  
Additionally, the potential benefits from certain initiatives were developed based on a pre-
pandemic workplan, which now needs to be adjusted to reflect National Grid’s current 
plans.  Moreover, should there be a second wave of the pandemic, certain non-essential 
work could again be paused, further impacting the Accelerate Program. 
2. 
The Accelerate Program was refreshed in June 2020.  Please see Attachment 1 (Wave 
changes communication) for changes introduced to make the Wave tool more effective 
and easier to track progress against FY21 targets.

FY21 Wave changes and workstream impacts 
1. Use FY20 baseline for new initiatives 
x
Problem addressed: It is difficult to calculate savings off an aging FY18 baseline, and we are unable 
to track efficiencies on new costs that did not occur in FY18 baseline. 
x
Workstream impact: Workstreams should begin using an FY20 baseline for new initiatives. Existing 
initiatives can either continue using an FY18 baseline or switch to an FY20 baseline. 
o
There is a new “Cost Occurrence” field on the Business Case tab of the initiative card. Select 
FY20 in this field if the initiative is creating efficiency on a cost that did not exist in FY18 and 
previously would have been ineligible to enter in Wave. Existing initiatives and new 
initiatives that save on costs that occurred in FY18 should have FY18 selected in this field. 
2. Track only newly implemented (IL4) controllable and non-controllable efficiencies for 
opex against single-year FY21 targets. Do not include revenue or EBIT in Accelerate 
reporting. 
x
Problem addressed: 3-year Accelerate targets (set in FY19) made it difficult to track controllable cost 
savings to budgets. Tracking and reporting revenue and EBIT from new sources diluted the focus on 
customer cost impacts. 
x
Workstream impact: New “Realized Date” field on initiative card that shows when an initiative 
entered IL4. Initiatives with a realized date of FY21 will count towards FY21 Accelerate targets, 
initiatives that were in IL4 before January 1, 2020 will not count towards FY21 targets. 
3. Updated allocation areas to reflect current operating model 
x
Problem addressed: Wave allocation areas reference outdated FY18 operating model, leading to a 
complicated link between savings & budget and unclear accountabilities. 
x
Workstream impact: Most allocation areas were renamed, and the updated name should show up in 
existing initiatives where the old name was. 
o
The Property and Fleet allocation area and delivery accountability has been split from (Fin. & 
Bus. Services) Property & Fleet to (Finance) Property and (Business Services) Fleet. Specific 
instructions for updating these fields within initiatives will be sent to the affected 
workstreams and IOs soon. 
4. Unused fields hidden on the initiative card: # Milestone Owners, Summary, Planning 
Summary, SBP Initiative, Coach Assigned 
x
Problem addressed: Cluttered initiative card that distracted from important fields 
x
Workstream impact: Reach out to the Accelerate team if you used any of these fields and would like 
them unhidden.

Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpaper to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 33, Workpaper 2: 
1.
How did the Company determine if the severance pay that was provided for staffing 
reductions was based on the staffing review versus standard business practice severance 
pay? 
2.
The Company shows that the allocations to NMPC electric and gas are 14.8% and 3.0%, 
respectively.  What are these allocations based on and how were they calculated?  
Provide all calculations and supporting documentation. 
3.
Explain the accounting treatment used by NMPC to record the severance payments. 
4.
Provide the actual journal entries that were recorded on the Company’s books of record 
to account for the severance payments.  Include the full account name and the account 
numbers of the debits and credits. 
5.
Explain if the Company began amortizing the costs to achieve once severance payments 
were paid out.  If no, explain why not.  If yes, provide support that will demonstrate the 
amortization. 
6.
From the time each employee left the Company and until the start of the new Rate Year, 
the Company has, and will continue, to realize savings due to these employees’ 
separation from the Company.  Provide the amount of savings the Company will realize 
from the time each employee left the Company through June 30, 2021, broken out by 
labor expense and labor benefits. 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 11 of 272


--- Page 246 ---
Form 103  
Response:  
1.
National Grid has a severance plan that provides benefits for regular full-time or regular 
part-time eligible management employees who, for reasons beyond their control, do not 
have a position with the company and are involuntarily released without cause.  An 
employee must meet the eligibility requirements outlined in the plan to be eligible to 
receive severance pay.  
Employees whose positions were eliminated as a result of the initiatives associated with the 
Accelerate Program and who met the eligibility requirements received severance pay in 
accordance with the provisions of the severance plan. 
2.
A rate of 17.8% was applied for labor costs allocated from National Grid USA Service 
Company, Inc. (“Service Company”) to Niagara Mohawk.  This rate was sourced from 
Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 23, Workpaper 7, Page 2 of 
2 (Labor - Allocation Rates).  This allocation was further split between Niagara Mohawk 
electric (83%) and Niagara Mohawk gas (17%) reflecting the treatment in Exhibit __ (RRP-
11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 9, Workpaper 12.  The allocation rates above 
net to charges of Service Company costs to Niagara Mohawk of 14.8% for electric and 
3.0% for gas. 
3.
Niagara Mohawk accounts for severance payments as follows: 
If the Company plans to sever an employee and the circumstances of this severance meet the 
accounting criteria (e.g., whether the severance is part of a formal restructuring program), 
a reserve, or severance provision, would be booked and an expense taken to the income 
statement.  It may be months before the employee exits the Company. 
When severance monies are paid to the employee on exit, this cash outflow is also booked to the 
income statement. 
On a monthly basis, the accounting team will review the severance provision, reversing any entries 
to the income statement that have been settled in cash. 
4.
Accounting entries, reflecting the accounting treatment detailed in the response to part 3, 
above, are: 
At the point at which we meet accounting criteria: 
Dr Separation Pay (Income Statement) C6001400 
Cr Severance provision C2426014 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 12 of 272


--- Page 247 ---
Form 103  
At the point at which severance is paid to an employee previously reserved: 
Dr Separation Pay (Income Statement) C6001400 
Cr Cash C1310000 
Monthly review of provision to reverse entries paid 
Dr Severance provision C2426014 
Cr Separation Pay (Income Statement) C6001400 
If we have not reserved for the employee then the entry is as follows: 
Dr Separation Pay (Income Statement) C6001400 
Cr Cash C1310000 
5.
The Company’s accounting for severance costs follows accounting guidance that ensures 
a charge is taken to the income statement when stated criteria are met.  If these criteria are 
not met, the charge is taken to the income statement when cash is paid to the employee.  
Therefore, severance costs are not amortized or spread over numerous accounting periods.  
Note that the three-year amortization of severance costs included in Exhibit __ (RRP-11), 
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 33, Workpaper 1, is for revenue requirements 
purposes only and does not represent the Company’s formal accounting policy. 
6.
The Company disagrees with the premise of the question that the Company has realized 
savings from employee separations that are incremental to the level of savings reflected in 
the Company’s current rates.  The 2017 Niagara Mohawk Rate Case imputed a significant 
level of unidentified efficiencies, including a one percent productivity adjustment in RY1, 
a 1.25 percent productivity adjustment in RY2, and a 1.25 percent productivity adjustment 
in RY3.  This imputation of unidentified efficiencies was over and above a further 
imputation of productivity savings equating to 20 basis points per year.  Therefore, it is the 
Company’s position that any labor savings related to severances were a means to achieve 
these unidentified efficiencies.  Notwithstanding, the cumulative “savings” on labor 
expense created from employees leaving the Company from the date of their exit to June 
30, 2021, was $2.9 million for Niagara Mohawk electric and $0.6 million for Niagara 
Mohawk gas.  Related labor benefits are $0.7 million for Niagara Mohawk electric and 
$0.1 million for Niagara Mohawk gas.  Please see Attachment 1 for workings and 
assumptions.

explained, teams were tasked with brainstorming initiatives to deliver process

SUBJECT:   
Federal Income Tax Audit of National Grid North America, Inc. (National Grid NA) 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall be 
construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet models in 
original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
1.
On pages 138 to 139 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Panel 
proposes to defer for future recovery from customers the interest expense incurred by the 
Company as a result of the resolution of a federal income tax audit of National Grid NA for the 
fiscal years ending March 31, 2010 through March 31, 2012. 
a.
Provide copies of any reports or presentations provided to the Board of Directors or 
senior management in regard to the federal income tax audit of National Grid NA. 
b.
Provide the calculation of the interest expense in the amount of $19.8 million and $4.9 
million for electric and gas, respectively, that the Company proposes to defer and recover 
from customers in the future. 
2.
On page 139 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Panel indicates that 
the Company’s taxable income for the three fiscal years, 2010, 2011, and 2012, with respect to 
the repair adjustment was increased by $139.8 million and the Company was required to pay 
additional taxes of $48.9 million. 
a.
Provide the calculation and supporting documentation for the increase in taxable income 
in the amount of $139.8 Million. 
b.
Provide the calculation and supporting documentation for the additional taxes of $48.9 
million. 
c.
Provide documentation demonstrating the Company paid the additional taxes of $48.9 
million. 
3.
On page 139 of the Direct Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Panel indicates that 
customers received the benefits associated with the repairs deduction and therefore it is 
appropriate for the Company to be allowed to defer interest costs arising from the subsequent 
reversal of the deduction that gave rise to the benefits.  Provide supporting documentation 
demonstrating that customers received the benefits associated with the repair deduction that was 
ultimately determined to be taken in error.

Form 103  
Response:  
1.
a.
There were no presentations or reports made to the Board of Directors or Senior 
Management regarding the settlement of the federal income tax audit of National Grid 
North America, Inc. and Subsidiaries for fiscal years ending March 31, 2010 to March 
31, 2012. 
b.
Please see Attachment 1 for the calculation of the federal and state interest expense in the 
amount of $19.8 million for electric and $4.9 million for gas. 
2.
a.
Please see Attachment 2-1 and Attachment 2-2.  Attachment 2-1, Form 5701, shows a 
total audit repair adjustment of $259.3 in consolidation.  Attachment 2-2 is a split of the 
repair deduction disallowance by company and shows Niagara Mohawk’s portion of 
taxable income increase of $139.8 million and the segment split. 
b.
Please see Attachment 2-2 for the calculation of the additional federal income taxes of 
$48.9 million.   
c.
Please see Attachment 2-2 for the journal entry of the federal intercompany cash 
settlement.  The total audit settlement is $75,230,080 but the Company is only requesting 
recovery of the interest expense related to the repair deduction disallowance of 
$48,941,154.  
Please see Attachment 2-3, the amended New York state tax return for fiscal year ending 
March 31, 2012, the year of the repair disallowance.  The amended return is required to 
be filed, after settlement of the IRS audit, to flow the federal adjustments through to state 
taxable income.  The return resulted in additional state tax of $9,750,120 and interest of 
$8,684,100.  Please see Attachment 2-4 for the check including tax and interest of 
$18,434,220. 
3.
Please see Attachment 3 for support demonstrating that customers received the benefits 
associated with the repair deduction that was ultimately reversed.  The table presents the time 
periods when the deferred tax liability associated with the deduction was included as a reduction 
to rate base and thus provided a benefit to customers.

Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 2, Workpaper 1, the 
Company includes $264,450 of costs related to Alix Partners, LLC. 
1.
Provide copies of all the invoices that support the costs related to Alix Partners, LLC in 
the amount of $264,450. 
2.
Provide the actual accounting applied (e.g., originating company, receiving order, 
purchase order number, allocation code, allocation percent to NMPC electric and gas, 
allocation methodology) so that verification of costs incurred can be reconciled with the 
Historic Test Year workpapers provided in Exhibit__(RRP-11). 
3.
Explain the nature of these costs and why the Company incurred them. 
4.
Provide copies of the purchase orders that support and identify the work being performed. 
5.
Explain whether or not these costs will recur during the Rate Year. 
Response:  
1-2. 
Please see Attachments 1 and 2 for the invoice supporting the costs related to Alix Partners, 
LLC and the associated accounting data, along with the tie-in to Exhibit__  (RRP-11), 
Workpapers to RRP-3, Schedule 1, Workpaper 1.  Please note the amount selected by Staff 
represents only the amount of this invoice allocated to Niagara Mohawk electric 
distribution.  Additionally, please note that the intended amount selected by Staff is 
“264,250,” as confirmed with Staff on September 22, 2020.  
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 122 of 272


--- Page 357 ---
Form 103  
3. 
The Company retained AlixPartners LLP to provide services aimed at ensuring the efficient 
delivery of the IT portfolio.  The work included, among other things, identifying IT 
efficiency opportunities; providing strategic support to the Cybersecurity team; change 
management support; analytical support to enhance IT internal performance metrics; and 
commercial support aimed at finding ways to lower vendor spend and improve 
performance.   
4. 
Please see Attachment 3 for a copy of the purchase order that supports the invoice 
requested. 
5. 
Over the last several years, the Company’s investments in IT have grown to meet the needs 
of modern energy networks that increasingly rely on state-of-the-art information systems 
to monitor, manage, and optimize system performance, integrate renewables and other 
distributed resources, and stay ahead of emerging cyber-security threats – all in a manner 
that mitigates costs to customers.  To accomplish these objectives, the Company, like all 
utilities today, utilizes consultants such as AlixPartners LLP to provide expertise aimed at 
ensuring the efficient delivery of the IT portfolio.  In that regard, the commercial support 
services performed by AlixPartners LLP resulted in the successful renegotiation of two 
vendor contracts, resulting in significant cost reductions for customers.  Specifically, the 
calendar year 2019 run rate savings from these efforts totaled approximately $6.8 million, 
with $7.019 million in savings reflected in the Rate Year revenue requirement (see
Accelerate Program initiatives nos. 944 and 945 in Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to 
Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 33, Workpaper 1).  The Company will continue to engage the 
services of consultants such as AlixPartners LLP in the Rate Year and beyond to look 
proactively for ways to maintain existing efficiencies, ensure the effective operation of the 
IT portfolio, stay abreast of cyber security concerns, and look continually for ways to 
improve overall IT performance.  Such work is reasonable and prudent and would be 
expected of any major company with an IT portfolio as large as the Company’s – especially 
given the potential benefits that could accrue to customers from this work.  For these 
reasons, these costs will recur in the Rate Year and Data Years.

Accelerate Overview
IL4 & IL5 approval requirements
Approval Requirementfor IL4
•
Complete all milestones
•
Implement initiative
•
Defined as business completing all activity required to deliver benefit
•
Develop methodology and evidence ability to identify and track savings on a monthly
basis against actual cost data
•
Benefits must be specifically factored into budget targets and therefore teams
cost and performance commitment.
•
Assess the regulatory impact of the initiative
•
Ensure benefits are visible and will be correctly treated in regulatory filings
Approval Requirementfor IL5
•
Once an initiative progresses to IL4 the focus is on determining whether actual
benefits, as identified through the monthly reporting process, are delivering forecast
•
After successive months of successfully demonstrating the above, benefits
generated by the initiative are consideredrealized and the initiative can move to IL5
•
This is a Finance function determination, reflected in the reductionto the
approval pool
•
Approval to IL5 means the initiative is consideredembedded in the cost base which
reduces the need for detailed ongoing tracking and enables Finance to focus on
demonstrating benefits from higher risk initiatives still in IL4

2.
Please see Attachment 1 for the requested information.  Note that the WAVE tool has been 
utilized to determine the extent to which savings, projected for fiscal year (“FY”) 2021, 
have already been captured in the Historic Test Year (“HTY”). Labor-related savings 
occurring during the HTY are assumed to be captured at the full annual run rate reflecting 
labor costs in the case applying a December 2019 headcount.  Non-labor savings during 
the HTY are captured as realized.  The majority of initiatives (including #842) are 100% 
labor-related.  Initiative #5568 is the one exception with 99% of savings being realized in 
the HTY, with 68% relating to headcount.  Exhibit___(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit 
RRP-3, Schedule 33, Workpaper 1 applied the simplifying assumption that 100% of the 
savings were captured through reduced headcount where a more accurate representation 
would be to split this between reduced headcount and embedded lower costs in the HTY.  
This is purely presentational, however, and has no impact to the revenue requirement.   
3.
As noted in the table above, the savings from this initiative relate to not hiring for an open 
position, with the requisition cancelled in January 2019.  The requirement to demonstrate 
and track savings caused the delay in approval to implementation level 4.   
4.
Please refer to the response to DPS-771, part 1. for details on the requirements for an 
initiative to be approved to implementation level 5.  Approval to implementation level 5 is 
determined by the Finance function and occurs when benefits have been successfully 
tracked over successive months demonstrating that forecast benefits have been realized.    
For initiatives that have resulted in reduced headcount, the Finance function typically 
monitors ongoing benefits over several months to ensure they are sustainable, are not being 
offset by incremental costs elsewhere, and are not the result of seasonal variation.  Please 
see the table below for comments on specific initiatives.

Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Exhibit__(RRP-11) Workpapers to RRP-3, Schedule 23, Workpaper 3 includes the following 
NMPC employee count as of December 31, 2019:  
• 
609 Total Management Employees   
• 
3,306 Total Represented Employees 
In reference to the Company’s response to IR DPS-477, Attachment 1, explain why the NMPC 
employee count for December 2019 (609 Total Management Employees and 3,278 Total 
Represented Employees) does not match the employee count in Exhibit__(RRP-3). 
Response:  
The numbers referenced from Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to RRP-3, Schedule 23, 
Workpaper 3 and DPS-477 Attachment 1 (609 Management and 3,278 Represented) are not raw 
employee count; they are numbers of full-time equivalents.  The corresponding raw employee 
counts are shown in Column BT of DPS-477 Attachment 1 .   
There are two drivers of the differences between Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to RRP-3, 
Schedule 23, Workpaper 3 and DPS-477 Attachment 1.  The first difference is caused by 
temporary employees, which are excluded in the Company’s response to DPS-477. 
The second difference is the calculation to convert the raw employee count of part-time 
employees to full-time equivalents.  The HR data presented in the Company’s response to DPS-
477 calculates each part-time employee as 0.5 full-time equivalents.  Exhibit __ (RRP-3), 
Schedule 23, the Labor model, calculates full-time equivalents on a prorated basis, using the 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 138 of 272


--- Page 373 ---
Form 103  
average salary per part-time employee, divided by the average salary per the corresponding full-
time employee, multiplied by the actual part-time employee count at December 31, 2019, as 
shown on Page 14 of 31 of Exhibit ___ (RRP-11), Workpapers to RRP-3, Schedule 23, 
Workpaper 3.
