SUBJECT:   Other Taxes Expense 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Referring to Exhibit__(RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit__(RRP-5) Schedule 3, Workpaper 1 the 
Company notes that the Historic Test Year was adjusted to remove the impact of a prior period 
completed Sales Tax Audit.  
1.
Provide all the documentation related to the sales tax audit referenced in the Company’s 
Workpaper. 
2.
Did the Company receive a refund as a result of the Sales Tax Audit?  If so, explain how 
the Company recorded the refund on its books of record. 
3.
If the Company has not received a refund yet explain how the Company intends to record 
the refund on its books of record. 
Response:  
1.  
On Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit (RRP-5) Schedule 3, Workpaper 1, the 
Company notes that the Historic Test Year was adjusted to remove the impact of a prior 
period completed Sales Tax Audit.  This footnote was inadvertently attributed to both 
Sales Tax Reserve and Sales & Use Tax.  The footnote only applies to the Sales Tax 
Reserve of $3,014,162, which was required to bring the reserve balance to zero.  As 
reflected in Attachment 1, any overpayments of sales tax identified during the audit were 
applied to offset any underpayments of sales tax, such that the net balance due on the 
audit was zero. 
The $467,676 adjustment to the Sales & Use Tax unintentionally included other Sales & 
Use tax items including URD and SUT.  The adjustment should be $615,445 ($506,795 
in electric and $108,650.24 in gas), which results in an understatement of the Historic 
Test Year(“HTY) of $327,205 in electric and $130,653 in gas.  Inflating the HTY 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 146 of 272


--- Page 381 ---
Form 103  
understatement to Rate Year 1, Data Year 1 and Data Year 2 results in an electric 
understatement of approximately $108,224, $110,819 and $113,524, respectively and a 
gas understatement of approximately $35,149, $45,280 and $46,385, respectively. 
2.   
No.  The Company did not receive a cash refund from the NYS Department of Taxation 
and Finance related to any overpayments of sales tax that were identified during the Sales 
Tax Audit.  During the course of a sales tax audit, the NYS Department of Taxation and 
Finance will identify underpayments of tax, as well as consider areas of overpayment.  As 
reflected in Attachment 1, any overpayments of sales tax identified during the audit were 
applied to offset any underpayments of sales tax, such that the net balance due on the 
audit was zero. 
3.  
Please refer to the Company’s response to Part 2 above.

NIAGARA MOHAWK POWER CORPORATION d/b/a NATIONAL GRID 
Case Nos. 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381 
Electric and Gas Rates 
Request for Information 
FROM: 
DPS Staff, Sarah Keymel 
TO: 
 
National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel 
SUBJECT:   Accelerate Program (Savings) 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
1.
Referring to the Company’s response to IR DPS-356, Attachment 3, page 8, the 
Company illustrates the various implementation phases and when savings are achieved 
for each of the initiative levels (i.e., level 3 initiatives, the Company is developing a 
detailed implementation plan, level 4 initiatives, all activities in the implementation plan 
are completed, and level 5 initiatives, value capture has been confirmed).  Provide more 
detail explaining the differences between implementation level 3, implementation level 4 
and implementation level 5 (including, but not limited to, at what level does 
implementation of the initiative begin, what is the lowest level savings can first be 
realized). 
2.
In the Company’s response to IR DPS-610, the Company stated in regard to the 
implementation status for some of the initiatives as “Initiative is implemented.  The focus 
is now on developing a methodology to determine if savings were achieved and, if so, 
how to track savings.”  If these initiatives have been implemented, while the Company is 
in the process of developing a methodology to determine if savings were achieved, could 
the Company already be realizing the savings from these initiatives?  Explain the 
Company’s reasoning. 
Response:  
1.
See below for details on approval requirements, development actions, and potential for 
realized savings as an initiative moves through implementation levels 3, 4, and 5.   
Implementation Level 3
Approval requirement (to get to current implementation level) 
• 
The initiative has a detailed implementation plan
• 
Key aspects of this implementation plan are entered in WAVE as milestones
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 155 of 272


--- Page 390 ---
Form 103  
• 
Typically, between five and ten milestones are established; however, this is not the 
entire project implementation plan
• 
A mechanism is developed to track (operational as well as financial) impact delivery 
Development actions (for approval to next implementation level) 
• 
The initiative begins its implementation phase/the project plan is being enacted 
• 
Progress against the implementation plan is tracked against milestones entered in 
WAVE 
• 
All milestones must be completed before approval to implementation level 4 
• 
Completion of all milestones does not automatically result in approval to 
implementation level 4 as milestones do not always represent a comprehensive 
project plan  
Potential for realized savings 
• 
At this stage, the business is taking actions to implement the initiative 
• 
Not every initiative will be successful 
• 
Whether an initiative has been successful in realizing savings is determined through 
the tracking and verification activity undertaken during implementation level 4 
• 
If realized savings are established and the initiative is approved to implementation 
level 5, then, with hindsight, the date these savings commenced could have been 
when the initiative was in implementation level 3 (i.e., after the initiative was 
implemented). Absent full implementation of the initiative and an analysis of 
whether actual savings resulted from the initiative, any savings at this stage are 
speculative at best.
Implementation Level 4 
Approval requirement (to get to current implementation level) 
• 
Complete all milestones 
• 
Implement the initiative, defined as business completing all activities required to 
deliver financial benefit 
• 
Develop a methodology and evidence the ability to identify, allocate, and track 
savings on a monthly basis against actual cost data 
• 
Benefits must be specifically factored into budget targets and therefore teams cost and 
performance commitment 
• 
Assess the regulatory impact of the initiative, ensuring benefits are visible, are 
correctly allocated, and will be correctly treated in regulatory proceedings 
Development actions (for approval to next implementation level) 
• 
Determine whether actual benefits, as identified through the monthly reporting 
process, are delivering the forecast 
• 
Determine whether the initiative has created a genuine reduction in the overall cost-
base of the business   
Potential for realized savings 
• 
At this stage savings are being monitored on a month by month basis
• 
Assuming the initiative is successful (i.e., actual benefits are delivering forecast), then 
realized savings are being generated throughout this stage 
Implementation Level 5 
Approval requirement (to get to current implementation level) 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 156 of 272


--- Page 391 ---
Form 103  
• 
After successive months of successfully demonstrating that forecast savings have 
been delivered, benefits generated by the initiative are considered realized 
• 
This is a Finance function determination and reflected in the reduction to the approval 
pool  
• 
Approval to implementation level 5 means the initiative is considered embedded in 
the cost base 
Development actions (for approval to next implementation level) 
• 
Not applicable 
Potential for realized savings 
• 
Ongoing savings are considered fully realized 
2.
See the description regarding implementation level 3 above.  A fundamental output of the 
Accelerate process is the requirement to demonstrate that a genuine reduction in the cost-
base has occurred as a direct result of the initiative.  This part of the process can take 
several months of analysis that necessarily happens after the initiative has been 
implemented.  A successful initiative may (but not necessarily) have started to realize 
savings when it was still in implementation level 3, after it had been fully implemented 
and the Company was undertaking the steps to determine if any savings had been 
achieved.  Many initiatives that are currently in implementation level 3, however, will not 
be able to demonstrate that savings have been realized, will not progress to successive 
implementation levels, and will ultimately be cancelled.  The Accelerate process needs to 
run its course before the correct determination can be made whether genuine savings 
have been realized.  This is why the Company believes that only savings in 
implementation levels 4 and 5 are appropriate to include in the revenue requirements.

1.
The Company incurred charges labeled “BUILDING EXPENSES AND SMALL TOOLS 
- DIST” in the amount of $0.562 million in calendar year (CY) 2019, $0.365 million in 
CY 2018, and $0.283 million in CY 2017. 
a.
Provide a description of the charges. 
b.

2019) is much greater than the amounts incurred in CY 2018, and CY 2017. 
2.
The Company incurred charges labeled “Conduct Operation Performance Analysis &” in 
the amount of $0.252 million in CY 2019, $0.021 million in CY 2018, and $0.001 million 
in CY 2017. 
a.
Provide a description of the charges. 
b.
Explain why the amount for charges incurred in the Historic Test Year (CY 2019) 
is much greater than the amounts incurred in CY 2018, and CY 2017. 
3.
The Company incurred charges labeled “Missing Home Cost Center Settlements” in the 
amount of $0.241 million in CY 2019. 
a.
Provide a description of the charges. 
b.
Explain why the Company believes these charges will occur during the Rate Year. 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 158 of 272


--- Page 393 ---
Form 103  
Response:  
1.  
In reference to charges “BUILDING EXPENSES AND SMALL TOOLS – DIST”: 
a.
The charges relate to safety personal protection equipment (PPE) needed to 
perform work and keep employees safe. 
b.
The amount for the charges incurred in CY 2019 is greater than prior years due to 
the need for incremental safety PPE.  The Company purchased approximately 190 
AED units and burn kits for approximately 600 trucks. 
2.  
In reference to charges labeled “Conduct Operation Performance Analysis &”: 
a.
The Company purchased a variety of materials related to gas main service (i.e.,
pipes, gaskets, leak detection liquid fluid, etc.) that are not specific to a single 
work type.  These materials are used during the installation/replacement of gas 
main and services. 
b.
The amount of charges incurred in CY 2019 is greater than the amounts incurred 
in CY 2018 and CY 2017 due to the use of an incorrect order that the Company 
discovered in preparing this response.  These charges were related to 
KEDNY/KEDLI and incorrectly charged to Niagara Mohawk.  The amount of the 
adjustment that should be made is $0.251 million.   
3. 
In reference to charges labeled “Missing Home Cost Settlements: 
a.   
The charges in “Missing Home Cost Center Settlements” represent system 
generated entries done as a true up of the FI-CO reconciliations.  These 
adjustments are discrepancies found between the FI system (Financial 
Information) and CO system (Controlling Module).  The discrepancies are the 
result of processes that ran incompletely or inaccurately and resulted in 
incorrectly configured master data.  The entries are made to true up the two 
modules as a result of the discrepancies.  The adjustments are made at a General 
Ledger account level resulting in adjustments with no underlying data such as 
order number or cost center.  
b.  
These costs will recur in the Rate Year as they are part of the process to reconcile 
the two SAP/BI systems and are part of the normal course of business.

a.
The group primarily affected by the Whitepaper’s proposed change in Section 
4(b) is the Company’s Instrumentation and Regulation (“I&R”) group.  Currently, 
I&R has employees performing work under the supervision of an operator 
qualified individual as part of its work plan and training program.  Staff’s 
proposal in Section 4(b) states that “[u]nder no circumstance may a not fully 
qualified individual perform covered tasks involving critical functions (pressure 
regulation, etc.), even if directed and observed by a qualified individual.”  This 
would prohibit all field work by an unqualified employee, even if performed 
under the direct supervision of a fully qualified employee.  At a high level, the 
Company estimates that, if adopted, the proposal in Section 4(b) would require 
approximately 20 new FTEs in the I&R group alone. 
b.
The new employees would need to be hired at least two years in advance of the 
need in the field as the Company would no longer be able to perform on the job 
training. 
c. 
The Company does not have an estimated cost associated with Section 4(b) 
implementation at this time, which is why a deferral was proposed in the event 
Section 4(b) is adopted.

3.

Refer to the Company’s response to IR DPS-773 for the following questions: 
6. 
The Company indicates that for initiative #824 five positions were eliminated after the 
Historic Test Year and for initiative #5460 one position was eliminated after the Historic 
Test Year. 
a.
Explain how the savings for both of these initiatives have been fully reflected in 
the revenue requirements, when these positions were eliminated after the Historic 
Test Year. 
b. 
For each of the six eliminated positions, provide the total labor and benefits 
savings associated with each position. 
7. 
Attachment 1 shows an amount of $6.294 million for “CY19 Actual Savings (Total)” and 
an amount of $6.689 million for “CY19 Actual Savings (Labor).”  Explain how the labor 
savings can be higher than the total savings in calendar year 2019. 
Response:  
1.
The Company utilizes third-party vendors (NCI and iQor) to handle collections calls.  
This initiative sought to reduce the amount of non-substantive time spent by the vendors 
on these calls.  To that end, the Company implemented an online tool enabling customers 
to enter and verify data online rather than over the telephone with the third-party vendor 
agent.  This has created a quicker and more streamlined process, improving the customer 
experience. Because NCI and iQor bill on a fixed unit cost basis, the initiative, while 
delivering qualitative benefits to customers through enhanced satisfaction, has not 
resulted in any direct savings to the Company.    
The Company, however, considers these fixed unit costs to be lower than the Company 
could achieve by bringing the activity in-house and this view has not changed with 
successful implementation of this initiative. These contracts were put in place before the 
start of the Historic Test Year so any benefits are fully reflected in the revenue 
requirement. 
As previously explained, a principal requirement for an initiative to move to 
implementation level 4 is to demonstrate measurable savings against a baseline of 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 165 of 272


--- Page 400 ---
Form 103  
FY2018 costs.  As the Company did not achieve cost reductions from this initiative, the 
initiative has not, and will not, move to implementation level 4.    
2.
Initiative #24734 relates to a study evaluating fleet utilization using GPS tracking 
technology. The initiative provided data on vehicle usage allowing the Company to 
optimize the size of its fleet.  As a result of this initiative, the fleet servicing the NY 
region was reduced by 28 vehicles during July and August 2019.  This realized both one-
time and enduring financial benefits through sales proceeds and reduction of running 
costs respectively. 
a.
Transportation expense is forecast using a detailed plan based on expected 
vehicles usage rather than simply inflating the Historic Test Year costs.  As 
shown in Exhibit ___ (RRP-3), Schedule 24, forecast costs are calculated by 
applying fuel, lease, and maintenance related unit costs to the number of vehicles 
estimated to be in service during the Rate Year. This estimate excluded the 29 
vehicles removed as a result of initiative #24734. 
b. 
As explained above, the Company does not use the Historic Test Year to forecast 
transportation; rather, this expense is discretely forecast based on anticipated fleet 
usage.  Further, as explained in DPS-874, initiatives are typically implemented by 
the business during implementation level 3.  Initiative #24734 was implemented 
in July and August 2019.  Therefore, when developing the forecast for 
transportation, the Company reflected the vehicle reductions from initiative 
#24734 – just as it did in the 2019 KEDNY/KEDLI Rate Cases.   
3.
One-time management and weekly labor savings relate to one-time, non-recurring labor 
related benefits realized in the Historic Test Year.  Examples of one-time, non-recurring 
labor related benefits realized in the Historic Test Year include items such as delayed 
hiring plan and overtime reduction.  
4.
As detailed in DPS-772, labor savings are entered into the WAVE tool excluding an 
uplift for benefits.  An uplift to include benefits is then applied, calculated net of any 
amounts already embedded in the Historic Test Year.  Any initiatives that generated one-
off labor savings in the Historic Test Year would overstate this deduction; therefore, they 
have been removed through the one-time management and weekly labor savings 
adjustment described above. 
5.
Ongoing benefits relating to this initiative have been omitted from the WAVE tool in 
error. Savings of approximately $1 million are projected for FY 2021 and will be 
included in the next monthly update to DPS-337.  Note this will not impact the revenue 
requirement as this benefit is already fully embedded through lower costs in the Historic 
Test Year.  
6.
Initiative #824 relates to generating efficiencies through the input of time data for electric 
operation employees across both the NY and NE jurisdictions. The first wave of 
implementation happened in NY.  The five positions eliminated after the Historic Test 
Year relate to NE employees with no allocation to Niagara Mohawk. 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)

--- Page 401 ---
Form 103  
With respect to initiative #5460, the position eliminated after the Historic Test Year 
included an allocation to Niagara Mohawk.  The salary was $45K with approximately 
$12K in benefits.  32.3% of the cost would have been allocated to Niagara Mohawk (split 
23.6% electric, 8.7% gas). Therefore, $19K was assumed fully embedded in the Historic 
Test Year in error and will be adjusted in the next monthly update to DPS-337. 
7.
This relates to initiatives #15784 and #15988, the creation of a capital delivery 
organization in electric and transmission, respectively.  These initiatives resulted in 
additional opex costs in CY2019 (to create the organization) offsetting savings from other 
initiatives.  Half of these additional costs were labor related, creating a lower reduction to 
net labor savings compared to the overall total.

2.
“Replacement interval of 7 years” is a high-level reference to planned replacement ages.  
Based on replacement age criteria for each vehicle and equipment class, this is 
specifically calculated as 7.75 years on average.  Replacement intervals are re-assessed 
periodically using total cost of ownership modelling.  Modelling from a third-party utility 
fleet benchmarking and consulting company was used to inform current replacement 
criteria. 
The following table provides the average age at retirement for the three seven-year 
interval periods requested:

3.
In general, the Company plans to replace vehicles on the seven-year cycle, but actual 
replacement varies based on usage.  This causes natural fluctuations in required 
replacements on a yearly basis, which can result in patterns of a larger number of 
replacements in some years versus other years as represented by the data provided in 
response to Part 1 above.  These patterns are the result of effective management of the 
Company’s fleet to create efficiencies while maintaining safe and reliable operation of 
the fleet.  Regardless of either scenario (high replacement versus low replacement), a 
lease expense would be present in the rate years (either under the old lease or the new 
lease).  The Company monitors the fleet in terms of safety and reliability, as opposed to 
replacing a standardized amount within a given year.

In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall

Lines 4, 9, and 13 of Exhibit___(EVP-5CU) of the Electric Vehicle Panel’s Corrections and 
Updates filing shows that the Company anticipates total costs of $854,308 for the Marketplace 
and Self Service component, $1,632,197 for the Turnkey Install component, and $426,240 for 
the Managed Charging component of the Company’s proposed Residential EV Program during 
the Rate Year. 
Lines 38, 35, and 39 of Exhibit___(EVP-8CU) show $1,632,197 in “Estimated Total [Turnkey 
Install] Costs,” $301,631 of “Total Revenue Returned to Ratepayers to Offset Program Costs,” 
and $1,330,566 of “Ratepayers Net Costs” during the Rate Year. 
1.
Has the Company reflected the anticipated $301,631 in revenues returned to customers to 
offset program costs as part of its revenue requirement? 
a.
If the Company’s response is “yes,” explain how such revenues are reflected in 
revenue requirement and provide a citation to where such revenues are discussed 
in Company’s testimony or exhibits. 
b.
If not, explain why not. 
Lines 22, 19, and 23 of Exhibit___(EVP-9CU) show $599,040 in “Estimated Total [Managed 
Charging] Costs, $302,400 in “Revenue Returned to Ratepayers to offset program costs,” and 
$296,640 in “Ratepayers Net Costs” in the Rate Year, respectively. 
2.
Explain why the “Estimated Total [Managed Charging] Costs” shown in 
Exhibit___(EVP-9CU) does not match the Managed Charging program costs shown on 
Line 13 of Exhibit___(EVP-5CU).  Identify and explain the correct figure.

and Self Service] Costs, $39,107 in “Revenue Returned to Ratepayers to offset program costs,”

4.
Has the Company reflected the anticipated $39,107 in revenues returned to customers to 
offset Marketplace and Self Service program costs as part of its revenue requirement? 
a.
If the Company’s response is “yes,” explain how such revenues are reflected in 
revenue requirement and provide a citation to where such revenues are discussed 
in Company testimony or exhibits. 
b.
If not, explain why not. 
Response:  
The Company reflected revenue associated with the Residential Electric Vehicle Program in 
miscellaneous revenue as presented on Exhibit __ (E-RDP-2CU), Schedule 4, Page 1, line 85 
totaling $728,323 in the Rate Year.  The $728,323 is comprised of $302,400 associated with 
managed charging (Exhibit __ (EVP-9CU), line 19); $48,884 (Exhibit __ (EVP-7), line 22 + line 
29) associated with Marketplace & Self Service; and $377,039 (Exhibit __ (EVP-8CU), line 27 + 
line 28 + line 34) associated with Turnkey Install Revenue.  A summary is provided in the table 
below. 
After consideration of how the revenue associated with the Marketplace & Self Service and 
Turnkey Install initiatives is reflected in the Company’s revenue requirement, the Company 
believes the revenue should be removed and a mechanism established to reconcile and share the 
actual revenue received.  Also, the Company believes that the actual revenue received in the 
Managed Charging Program associated with fixed costs should be deferred for future pass back 
to customers.  Only the revenue associated with fixed costs and not variable will be passed back 
to customers because the variable costs are not included in the revenue requirement.  A summary 
is provided in the table below. 
Another revision concerns a mismatch between the costs presented on Exhibit __ (EVP-1CU) 
versus the costs included in the Company’s revenue requirement presented on Exhibit __ (RRP-
3CU), Schedule 27.  A revision to the revenue requirement is necessary to match costs presented 
on Exhibit __ (EVP-1CU) as shown in the note to the table below.

Form 103  
2.
Please see Attachment 2 for the support so the verification of costs incurred can be 
reconciled with the Historic Test Year workpapers provided in Exhibit__(RRP-11), 
Workpapers to Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 7, Workpaper 1. 
3.  
The charges represent the dues paid to the American Gas Association.  The Company 
incurred these charges to maintain membership in the American Gas Association, a 
leading organization in the gas industry.  Membership within the American Gas 
Association provides access to events such as workshops and seminars that provide the 
Company and its employees with invaluable opportunities to collaborate and share best 
practices among member utilities on issues impacting the gas industry, such as gas safety 
and operations, engineering, storm response, finance and accounting, energy efficiency, 
new technology, the integration of renewables into the gas network, and topics related to 
the future of heat. The Company uses these resources to aid in the provision of safe, 
reliable, and cost-effective service to customers.  Please note that only the non-lobbying 
component of AGA dues are included in the Company’s revenue requirement; the 
lobbying component is subsequently booked to the 426 FERC account, for which the 
Company is not seeking recovery. 
4.
There is no purchase order associated with these invoices.  
5.
The Company will maintain its American Gas Association membership and these costs 
will recur during the Rate Year and Data Years.

The only other correspondence with the IRS is the required disclosure under Revenue 
Procedure 94-69.  Attachment 1A is an excerpt from this disclosure, including all 
disclosed information about this issue.  This revenue procedure requires the taxpayer to 
disclose any known unfavorable adjustments to the IRS at the start of an audit of a tax 
period.  This issue was originally disclosed at the start of the audit for fiscal year ending 
March 31, 2009, and then again for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2012.  The IRS 
Form 5701 explains the rationale for the delay in auditing the issue.  
2.
Please refer to Attachment 2 for the journal entry to record the total interest paid as a 
result of the settlement of the federal income tax audit for the fiscal years ending March 
31, 2010, through March 31, 2012.  Please note that this entry relates to interest payable 
for all adjustments to taxable income for all years within the audit cycle.  The Company, 
however, is only proposing to defer for future recovery from customers interest expense 
related to the disallowance of repairs deduction. 
3.
a.
Please refer to Attachment 3 for support of the total repair deduction disallowance 
of $259,324,828 and the breakout of that adjustment by company, including the 
$139,831,869 pertaining to Niagara Mohawk.  The first section represents the 
results of the original study performed for the change in accounting method and 
ultimately the adjustment included in the fiscal year ending March 31, 2009 tax 
return.  The second section is the revised study performed after filing the tax 
return and is a more accurate calculation of the repair deduction adjustment.  The 
audit adjustment for fiscal year ending March 31, 2012, is the difference between 
the two. 
b.
The repair deduction disallowance is allocated to the electric and gas businesses 
using an 80 percent electric and 20 percent gas split.  The Company’s plant 
related accumulated deferred income tax balances (“ADIT”) have historically 
been tracking at these percentages. 
4.
a.
The $9,928,063 shown in Attachment 2-2 in response to DPS-678 represents the 
state income taxes specifically related to the increase in taxable income as a result 
of the disallowance of the repairs deduction for fiscal year ending March 31, 
2012.  The $9,750,120 of additional state income taxes paid shown on page 20 of 
Attachment 2-3 in response to DPS-678 is the total increase in the Company’s 
state income tax liability as a result of the resolution of the federal income tax 
audit for that same fiscal year.  In addition to the increase in taxable income 
resulting from the disallowance of the repairs deduction, there were other 
favorable adjustments included in the federal audit settlement that explain the 
difference between the one repair issue and the total return.  Please refer to 
Attachment 1 for a detailed breakdown of the total increase in taxable income, 
which includes the $139,831,869 of repairs deduction disallowance.

The total audit adjustments shown on Attachment 1 agrees to the increase in 
allocated combined business income on page 15 of Attachment 2-3 in response to 
DPS-678.   
b.
The Company used the $9,928,063 of income taxes to calculate the additional 
interest expense paid because that amount represents the state income tax impact 
of the disallowance of the repair deduction only rather than the additional tax due 
on the entire return.  The Company often has various favorable and unfavorable 
adjustments resulting from IRS audits but does not typically ask for recovery of, 
or proposed return of interest from, all of them as the amounts are too immaterial 
to track and over time the deferred tax impact is included in rate base, if 
appropriate.  If an audit resulted in a refund of over $1.5 million, the Company 
would file the required reconciliation that would explain the shareholder/customer 
disposition of such a refund, including interest.  The Company is asking for 
recovery of the interest related to this particular issue as the effects are material to 
rate base and earnings and the Company was required to return all repair related 
benefits to customers as soon as the refund was received on the original change in 
accounting method in 2009.   
5.
The $8,684,099.62 of additional interest paid shown on page 20 of Attachment 2-3 in 
response to DPS-678 is the total interest paid for all audit adjustments as result of the 
resolution of the federal income tax audit for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2012.  The 
$8,599,371 shown in Attachment 1 in response to DPS-678 pertains specifically to the 
interest related to the disallowance of the repair deduction.  The interest calculation 
included in Attachment 1, DPS-678 is based on an Excel file that the Company uses to 
record reserve related accrued interest on a quarterly basis.  The interest calculation 
included with the New York State return is from an interest calculation system and has a 
slightly different result. 
6.
a.
During the base rate filings in Cases 12-E-0201 and 12-G-0202, the starting point 
for ADIT was the total amount per books, which included the deferred tax 
liability for the full repair deduction taken on the FY 2009 tax return.  Please see 
Attachment 4, which is the ADIT calculation tab from the settlement file of those 
cases.  In October 2013, there was a repair adjustment taken to remove the 
deferred tax liability associated with the error.  In the electric ADIT calculation, 
$27,175,335 was removed from federal and $9,928,063 was removed from state.  
There were no adjustments in the gas segment.  At that time, the Company 
estimated that the federal audit would settle around that time and the accounting 
would be completed, so the ADIT adjustment was made to increase rate base.  
The Company did not file a full rate case with a reset of ADIT balances back to 
actuals until Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239, with new rates effective on April 1, 
2018.  In Attachment 5, the Company is revising Attachment 3 from DPS-678 to 
account for the adjustments to the electric segment and account for no rate base 
adjustments to the gas segment.

b.
The starting point for ADIT for each rate case is the historic test year ADIT 
exhibit.  The first columns of this exhibit are the full ADIT balance per the 
general ledger.  That amount is adjusted by the tax regulatory asset or liability 
balances, referred to as FAS 109 balances, and other rate case adjustments, which 
represent the reversal of the ADIT portion of tax reserves on temporary items plus 
the ADIT associated with other accounts not in rate base.  Because the ADIT 
balances represent an “as filed per tax return” balance, the full deduction for the 
2009 repairs was included in the deferred tax liability.  There is no specific 
adjustment for the deduction except as noted in the response to part a. above.  As 
the ADIT balance in Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239 were reset to the ledger 
balances and the federal audit adjustment accounting that reduced the ADIT credit 
was not done until December 2019, then those balances are included in present 
rates and will not be adjusted out until new rates go into effect in the present case, 
July 2021.  Attachment 6 is the ADIT exhibit from Cases 12-E-0201 and 12-G-
0202 and Attachment 7 is the ADIT exhibit from Cases 17-E 0238 and 17-G-
0239. 
c.
The Company is amending its request to defer for the recovery of interest paid on 
account of the settlement of the FY 2010-FY 2012 audit repair issue from the 
original amount of $24.7 million to the amount of $22.4 million.  Please see 
Attachment 5 for revised amounts.  At the time of the rate case filing, the 
Company had calculated the interest related to the repair adjustment based on 
interest rates for each fiscal period.  It was assumed, since there was a long period 
of time between the deduction and the settlement, that the benefits the customers 
received related to this issue would be more than the interest paid.  Upon 
investigation of various rate case filings, it was discovered that there was a 
significant gap period where customers did not receive the full benefit of this 
deduction.  The periods where customers did receive the benefit added up to a 
benefit of $22.4 million, which the Company views as the more appropriate 
amount to propose for recovery.

Nature/Explanation of Potential Controversy: 
 
1 Repairs Expense:  ($259,324,827) 
Prior to FY09, the Company followed regulatory accounting rules (for both and tax 
purposes) to report the capitalization, repair, and retirement of its electric transmission 
and distribution assets. Under this regulatory method, the Company made 
capitalization, repairs and retirement determinations with reference to granular units of 
property, causing many incidental repair and maintenance costs, properly deductible 
under Regulation section 1.162-4, to be capitalized improperly for tax purposes.    
 
In December 2009, the Company filed Forms 3115 to change its tax methods of 
accounting for the capitalization, repair, and retirement of its electric transmission and 
distribution assets; however, it continued following the regulatory method for book 
purposes.  Under the adopted tax method of accounting for capitalization and repairs, 
the Company generally defined its units of property as electric circuits and substations 
and made capitalization and repairs determinations with reference to those larger units 
of property.  Under the Company’s adopted tax method of accounting for retirements, 
the Company only recognized the retirement of an entire circuit or substation, not 
recognizing book retirements under the regulatory method which were merely partial 
dispositions with respect to those larger units of property. 
 
The Company reported a favorable §481(a) adjustment of $1,102,457,577 for the 
capitalization and repairs method change and unfavorable §481(a) adjustment of 
$127,922,504 for the retirement method change.   On its FY09 tax return (also filed in 
December 2009), the Company also deducted $478,990,341 of repairs which were 
capitalized for book purposes under the regulatory method.  The Company did not 
update tax basis data its PowerTax records for the impact of the §481(a) adjustments 
and the repairs deduction but did prepare off system calculations to adjust FY09 
depreciation deductions for these items. 
 
The Company later determined that the §481(a) adjustment reported on Forms 3115 
and the repairs and depreciation deductions claimed on the FY09 Form 1120 were not 
correct, resulting in an understatement of taxable income in FY09 by $259,324,827 
determined as follows:

The Company later updated its PowerTax depreciation records to reflect the corrected 
§481(a) adjustments and FY09 repairs and depreciation deductions.  Therefore, the 
Company will also be claiming additional depreciation deductions over the remaining 
life of the applicable assets which equal the understatement of taxable income in FY09. 
 
In August 2011, the IRS issued Rev. Proc. 2011-43 providing a safe harbor 
capitalization and repairs method of accounting for electric transmission and 
distribution property.  The Company adopted this method on a Form 3115 filed in 
December 2012 and reported an unfavorable §481(a) adjustment of $101,141,252 on 
its FY12 tax return.  This §481(a) adjustment was determined using the extrapolation 
provisions of Rev. Proc. 2011-43, Appendix A.  Corrections needed for the December 
2009 method change (as described above) were not included in the §481(a) adjustment. 
 
The Company disclosed the unfavorable adjustment for this issue during the FY08-09 
IRS examination.  The IRS exam team, as required in LB&I Directive 4-1111-019, 
declined to accept the adjustment.  (This LB&I directive instructed examiners to 
discontinue exam activity for capitalization and repairs issues related to Rev. Proc. 
2011-43 electric transmission and distribution property for all tax years ending before 
December 31, 2010.) 
 
The Company is resubmitting this adjustment for FY12, the tax year during which it 
filed Form 3115 to adopt Rev. Proc. 2011-43.

Refer to the Company’s response and attachments to IR DPS-892 for the following questions: 
1.
Explain what the term STI stands for, as used on page 4 of Attachment 4. 
2.
Provide the data for fiscal years 2012 through 2014, depicted as a graph similar to the 
graph on page 4 of Attachment 4. 
3.
Provide the total workers’ compensation claims and expense for fiscal years 2012 
through 2014, depicted as graphs similar to the graphs on page 5 of Attachment 5. 
4.
Provide a list and a brief description of all safety measures given to employees (e.g., 
safety moments before presentations, annual safety trainings).   
5.
Explain whether or not the Company continues to improve its employee safety programs, 
trainings, etc. over the years.  
6.
Provide information demonstrating that the reduction in worker’s compensation claims 
and expenses are directly tied to the Athletic Trainer Program provided by ATI Holdings. 
Response:  
1.
STI stands for Soft Tissue Injury.  More recently, the Company has been referring to this 
as musculoskeletal (“MSK”) injury.  
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 215 of 272


--- Page 450 ---
Form 103  
2.
Please see Attachment 1, which displays MSK injury by severity for Fiscal Years 2012 
through 2018.   
3.
Data for Fiscal Years 2012 and 2013 is not readily available absent a manual review of 
such data, which would be extremely time consuming and unduly burdensome.  Fiscal 
Year 2014 data was provided in DPS-892 Attachment 4. 
4.
Please see Attachment 2 for a current listing of the US Safety, Health & Environment 
initiatives and a brief description of each.  Please see Attachment 3 for a listing of 
courses and programs the Company offers annually, as well as additional safety measures 
taken by the Company to reduce soft tissue injuries.  
5.
The Company promotes a culture of safety, which is reflected in its courses and 
programs.  Please see Attachments 2 and 3 for a listing of these items undertaken by the 
Company to continue to promote the safety culture.  The Company continuously looks 
for ways to ensure a safe environment. 
6.
There are a multitude of variables that impact the number of workers’ compensation 
claims processed by the Company each year.  Factors such as number of hours worked, 
number, size, and complexity of work projects, weather conditions, safety program 
changes and new processes, athletic training, etc., as well as additional environmental 
factors may all impact safety statistics each year.  Therefore, it is not possible to quantify 
the specific effect of each individual program or factor on the number of injuries or 
workers’ compensation claims annually.  That said, as shown in Attachments 4 and 6 to 
DPS-892, the Athletic Trainer Program has helped contribute to a reduction in the 
number of workers’ compensation claims.

In addition to the Company's ATI program to reduce soft tissue injuries:
1- Field Safety choose an internal represented person to lead stretch and flex in gas operations as well as CMS. This occurs 
throughout the Eastern Division. This employee traveled every morning to a different location (pre-COVID).  He has also 
demonstrated his expertise at the Gas SPC in order for the wider organization to adopt this opportunity.  
In addition- Field Safety, CMS and Gas Operations made weekly stretch and flex videos. These videos demonstrated 
different types of stretching. Each weekly video was then distributed to each employee by text. Employees could view them 
prior to shifts.
2- Field Safety across the organization developed a soft tissue injury avoidance program. This program consisted of our 
folks, CMS and Gas Operations implementing a hands on piping simulator. We instructed employees with representatives of 
LU97 on how to position their bodies to avoid injury while using tools specifically pipe wrenches.
3- Field Safety participates and leads stretch and flex sessions in operating facilities as well as in the field.
4- Field Safety discusses appropriate body positioning while working in tight quarters. This could be in customer homes or 
excavations.

Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
1.
Referring to the Company’s response to IR DPS-885, the Company explains that the 
charges labeled “Miscellaneous Write-off Adjustments-9302” are “costs paid for the 
purchase of Bluetooth-enabled gas leak detectors for the Gas Business Unit.” 
a.
Provide the total number of Bluetooth-enabled gas leak detectors purchased for 
calendar year (CY) 2019.  
b.
Provide the number of Bluetooth enabled gas leak detectors purchased year-to-
date for CY 2020. 
c.
Identify the number of units needed to fulfill the Bluetooth-enabled gas leak 
detector program.  In addition, explain why the Company believes the number of 
Bluetooth-enabled leak detectors purchased in the Historic Test Year serves as a 
reasonable basis to forecast the Rate Year. 
d.
Provide a listing of invoices supporting the amount incurred in the Historic Test 
Year of $0.651 million. 
2.
Referring to the Company’s response to IR DPS-886, the Company explains that “The 
increase [in costs for vendor eAccess Solutions Inc.] from CY 2018 to CY 2019 is a 
result of the ramp up of the residential methane detector program.  As a result of the ramp 
up, there was the need to purchase more residential methane detectors.” 
a. 
Provide the total number of residential methane detectors purchased for CY 2019.

b.
Provide the number of residential methane detectors purchased year-to-date for

3.
Referring to the Company’s response to IR DPS-639, Attachments 2 and 3, the Company 
incurred charges from a vendor labeled “Not Assigned,” which contained charges 
classified as “CR Cancellation.” 
a. 
Explain what the charges classified as “CR Cancellation” represent. 
b.
The charges classified as “CR Cancellation” were approximately $0.113 million 
in CY 2017, $0.283 million in CY 2018, and $0.699 million in CY 2019.  The 
amount incurred in CY 2019 was 147% greater than the amount incurred in CY 
2018, and 516% greater than the amount incurred in CY 2017.  Explain the 
significant increase of the charges incurred in CY 2019, and why the Company 
believes this serves as a reasonable basis to forecast the Rate Year. 
Response:  
1.
a. 
In calendar year 2019, the Company purchased a total of 86 Bluetooth-enabled 
gas leak detectors.   
b.
Year to date for calendar year 2020, the Company purchased 154 Bluetooth-
enabled gas leak detectors.  Four additional units will be delivered in November 
for a total of 158 for calendar year 2020.  
c.
A total of 244 Bluetooth-enabled gas leak detectors will be needed to fulfill the 
program.  Rather than the spend for these specific detectors or this specific 
program recurring in the Rate Year, the Company expects the same level of spend 
will likely occur for another mandated/safety program in the normal course of 
business to maintain safe and reliable service to customers.  If the program spend 
is not for the purchase of gas leak detectors, then it will be for another 
mandated/safety program that requires the Company to purchase additional safety 
equipment.  Therefore, these costs will continue to be incurred in the Rate Year.   
d.
Please see below for a listing of document numbers that make up $0.651 million 
in “Miscellaneous Write Off Adjustments - 9302.” 
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)

Form 103  
2.  
a. 
In calendar year 2019, the Company purchased 40,014 residential methane 
detectors (“RMD”) units using the negative revenue adjustment (“NRA”) funding 
authorized in the Section 7.5.1 of the Joint Proposal adopted in Case 17-G-0239.   
b.
The Company has not purchased any residential methane detectors to date in 
calendar year 2020.   
c. 
The RMD Program adopted in Section 7.5.1 of the Joint Proposal was a limited 
scope program ending once the NRA funding was spent.  The Company 
completed its distribution of RMDs and filed its final status report closing the 
program on July 30, 2020.  Please see Attachment 1 for listing of all invoices for 
the purchased units and the final status report filed in Case 17-G-0239 closing the 
program. 
On January 14, 2020, the Company submitted a petition in Case 17-G-0239 
proposing an Incremental RMD Program to distribute an additional 21,600 RMDs 
beyond the RMDs approved in the Joint Proposal.  The Commission approved the 
Company’s petition on June 15, 2020 and authorized the Company to distribute of 
up to 64,800 RMDs using NRA funding through the Incremental RMD Program.  
Thus, any additional RMDs will be purchased as part of the Incremental RMD 
Program recently approved by the Commission on June 15, 2020.   
d.
The Company expects that these costs will continue to be incurred in the Rate 
Year based on the number of RMD units approved in the Commission’s June 
2020 order.  The Company notes that these costs would continue to be purchased 
with NRA funding. It should be noted the costs were deferred in the test year so 
are not reflected on the rate year revenue requirements. 
3.   
a. 
Charges that are classified as “CR Cancellation” are those costs that were 
captured on a capital work order but do not have any capital assets associated.  
The capital costs on these projects are transferred to expense.  In some cases, the 
capital costs are transferred to other work orders where the assets are located prior 
to the cancellation process running resulting in zero P&L impact.   
b.
In calendar year 2019, QinetiQ overhead line sensors were deployed throughout 
the distribution electrical system in New York.  The sensors were purchased 
under one work order and closed out under a different work order.  During the 
final closeout of the project in calendar year 2019, the Company identified that

In the Company’s response to IR DPS-337 (October 2020), the Company indicates that four 
initiatives (#33206, #33211, #33221, and #33231) have moved up to implementation level 4 
and that three of these initiatives’ savings (#33206, #33211 and #33221) have already been 
reflected in the revenue requirements. 
1. 
Explain in detail how the savings for these three initiatives have already been reflected 
in the revenue requirements. 
2. 
The Company has indicated the savings related to these four initiatives are the result of a 
reduction in headcount.  For each initiative, provide the date when each position was 
vacated. 
Response:  
1.
As explained in DPS-610 and DPS-771, these three initiatives were implemented by the 
business and the Company was working to determine if savings had been achieved.  That 
determination was made and these initiatives moved to implementation 4 in October 
2020.   
The implementation date of these initiatives and the date they started realizing benefits is 
as follows:

These initiatives relate to delivering the Company’s aspiration to increase distribution

factors impeding field crew productivity, which has enabled overhead line crews to 
complete more capital work with the available resources.  Because the initiatives were 
implemented before the end of the Historic Test Year, the resource levels fully reflect the 
benefits within the revenue requirement.  
2.
Although the benefits for these initiatives were coded as “headcount reduction,” these 
initiatives relate to realizing labor efficiencies enabling the Company to deliver its 
existing capital investment program efficiently.  Without this initiative, less overall 
construction would have been achieved for the same level of investment.  Additionally, 
as the capital investment plan has increased over the past several years, the Company has 
not increased its Distribution overhead line workforce.  Field Excellence was a critical 
initiative to continue to complete work efficiently while at the same time maintaining a 
safe and reliable system on behalf of customers.

FROM: 
DPS Staff, John Ross, Jr.

National Grid, Revenue Requirements Panel 
SUBJECT:   Transportation 
Request: 
Note:
In all interrogatories, all requests for workpapers or supporting calculations shall 
be construed as requesting any Word, Excel or other computer spreadsheet 
models in original electronic format with all formulae intact and unlocked. 
Based on the Company’s response to IR DPS-457, the average new leasing cost per 
replacement vehicle (i.e., dollar amount incurred for new leases divided by number of vehicles 
replaced) in calendar year (CY) 2017 was approximately $8,124, in CY2018 was approximately 
$10,584 per replacement vehicle, and in CY2019 was approximately $7,309 per replacement 
vehicle.  However, based on the Company’s response to IR DPS-745, the projection for the 
average new leasing cost per replacement vehicle through the end of the Rate Year is 
approximately $15,653.  Explain why the Company’s average leasing cost per vehicle 
forecasted through the Rate Year is much greater than what the Company has historically 
incurred. 
Response:  
The average leasing costs per vehicle, quoted in the question from Staff, are not comparable 
because the replacement counts and dollars measured are over different lengths of time (i.e., one 
year versus 2.5 years).  The Rate Year includes full year costs for replacements made in the 18 
months before the Rate Year as well as the partial year costs for replacements made in the Rate 
Year while the historic years only include the partial year costs for replacements in the particular 
historic year.  The Rate Year amounts that Staff used to calculate the $15,653 cost estimates are 
based on a dataset that includes 2.5 years (January 1, 2020, through June 30, 2022) of 
replacement volume and uses only the last twelve months of dollars to determine the Rate Year 
amount.  This means that, if a vehicle is replaced halfway through the first year, the total months 
in service is six months and the total replacement lease cost for that one year would be six 
months of lease payments.  When one looks at that same replacement lease for the last year of 
the 2.5-year period, it is a full twelve months of lease payments.   
Exhibit______(RRP-5R)
Page 230 of 272


--- Page 465 ---
Form 103  
Therefore, when one calculates total replacement lease costs in the last year of a 2.5-year period, 
the result includes a full twelve months of lease payments on any lease replaced in the first 18 
months of that 2.5 year period, or in this case, most of the leases.  The amounts calculated for 
CY2017, CY2018, and CY2019 are not comparable.  These amounts are calculated on 
replacements occurring during a one-year period only, meaning almost every lease in the total 
replacement lease cost for that year will have less than twelve months of lease payments (unless 
the lease was replaced in the first month).  This creates significant discrepancies in the average 
lease cost per vehicle calculation applied by the Staff and results in an unrealistic variance in the 
Rate Year when compared to CY2017, CY2018, and CY2019. 
Please see Attachment 1 for a hypothetical example to illustrate the above points.  
To account for this variation of months in service described above, an average monthly lease cost 
is the most appropriate comparison.  For each replacement, the total lease expense for the period 
is divided by the months in service in that period.  Then an average of all records in the period is 
taken to determine the average monthly lease costs, broken down by year, presented in the table 
below.  Please see Attachment 2 for line item detail. 
CY2017 
CY2018 
CY2019 
RY1 
$1,065 
$1,369 
$1,289 
$1,519 
The actual average monthly lease cost, as presented, is comparable to the time periods discussed 
above. 
The variation that remains in average monthly lease costs, across historical calendar years and 
the Rate Year, is predominantly driven by the asset mix, which in turn is driven by lifecycles and 
age/usage of the asset to be replaced. 
The variance driver for the Rate Year compared to CY2018 and CY2019 is primarily due to the 
volume of replacements in three specific classes of high cost vehicle classes (HD ATV 
Aerials/Diggers, Truck Mounted Digger Derricks, and Cranes).  All three of these classes include 
equipment that are replaced on a lifecycle of eight to ten years.  The lifecycle of these assets is 
driving the volume in RY1 based on the in-service dates of the units they are replacing. 
Count HD ATV Aerials/Diggers, Digger Derricks, and Cranes:

104 
If both the dollars and counts for these 104 high cost vehicle classes were removed from the 
average monthly lease cost calculation shown above, the new average monthly lease cost would 
be $1,307, which is more in line with both CY2018 and CY2019. 
The lower average monthly lease cost in CY2017 is driven by the mix of the 15 most expensive 
vehicle types (most expensive defined by average monthly cost).

National Grid, Miscellaneous 
SUBJECT:   Miscellaneous - AGA - Revenue Requirements - HTY Review
Request: 
53. 
Has National Grid been a member of the American Gas Association (“AGA”) at any time 
during the last three years? 
If yes, please identify the amount of annual membership dues National Grid has paid to 
AGA for each of the last three years National Grid was an AGA member. 
If yes, please identify the percentage of membership dues that National Grid charged to 
ratepayers and identify the basis for such cost recovery. 
Please identify the witness responsible for this answer. 
Response:  
Yes, National Grid has been a member of the American Gas Association (“AGA”) during the last 
three years. 
National Grid has paid AGA annual membership dues of: 
Calendar Year 2017:  $1,084,131 
Calendar Year 2018:  $1,138,338 
Calendar Year 2019:  $1,195,255 
The percentage of membership dues included in the revenue requirements are as follows: 
Calendar Year 2017:  93.6% 
Calendar Year 2018:  96.9% 
Calendar Year 2019:  96.5%

The basis for cost recovery of AGA Membership dues is the New York State Public Service 
Commission’s order establishing rates in Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239, which included the 
cost recovery of the non-lobbying portion of AGA Membership in the revenue requirement. 
The witness responsible for this answer is the Revenue Requirements Panel.

Request: 
54.  
Is National Grid seeking cost recovery for AGA membership dues during FY 2021 - 
2025? 
a. 
If yes, please identify the annual membership dues National Grid expects to pay 
to AGA in FY 2021, FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024, and FY 2025, the percentage 
of total membership fees for which National Grid seeks cost recovery, and all 
documentation supporting the basis for cost recovery. 
Response:  
National Grid is seeking cost recovery for the non-lobbying portion of AGA membership dues 
during the Rate Year ending June 30, 2022, and Data Years ending June 30, 2023 and June 30, 
2024 – these periods span portions of fiscal year (“FY”) 2022 through FY 2025.   
Please refer to Attachment 1 for the total forecast amounts for the non-lobbying portion of AGA 
dues. 
The forecast for these items is derived from the normalized Historic Test Year (“HTY”) and 
adjusted for inflation.  The percentage of total membership dues National Grid is seeking cost 
recovery for is 96.5% based on the non-lobbying portion presented on the AGA invoice during 
the HTY as seen in Attachment 2.  Please note these totals are for National Grid USA; the 
percentage allocated to Niagara Mohawk at the end of the Historic Test Year is 10.91%.

Request: 
55.  
Is National Grid seeking cost recovery for employees or representatives to attend AGA 
events in FY 2021, FY 2022, FY 2023, FY 2024, and FY 2025? If yes, please explain the 
total amount National Grid is seeking for these expenses and the basis for cost recovery. 
Response:  
Yes, the Rate Year and Data Years’ forecast includes costs associated with attending AGA non-
lobbying events.  The Company does not have a breakdown of these costs, as they are not 
tracked in a manner that would allow the Company to readily identify these items absent a 
burdensome and time-intensive manual review of individual employee expense invoices.  The 
basis for cost recovery is that AGA is a leading organization in the gas industry.  Events such as 
workshops and seminars provide the Company and its employees with invaluable opportunities 
to collaborate and share best practices among member utilities on issues impacting the gas 
industry, such as gas safety and operations, engineering, storm response, finance and accounting, 
energy efficiency, new technology, the integration of renewables into the gas network, and topics 
related to the future of heat.  The Company uses these resources to aid in the provision of safe, 
reliable, and cost-effective service to customers.

Subject: 
Labor – Vacancy Rates 
Question: 
Is it Staff’s position that there are no vacancies included in the December 31, 2019 headcounts 
used in Niagara Mohawk’s Rate Year labor expense forecast? 
Response: 
The SSRP’s position is that the Company did not account for vacancies for the period from the 
end of the Historic Test Year through the Rate Year in developing the Company’s Rate Year 
labor forecasts and the Company’s projected Rate Year incremental FTEs contained in the Other 
Initiatives expense cost element.  There is no testimony from the Company on vacancies and 
how the Company accounted for such vacancies within its Rate Year forecasts. 
As stated on page 32 of our testimony, with respect to NMPC itself, the NMPC active FTE level 
as of November 1, 2020 was 122.5 FTEs less than the Company’s adjusted headcount as of 
December 31, 2019.  Thus, based on the most recent data, the Company’s headcount is lower 
than the December 31, 2019 adjusted headcount, indicating that there are vacant positions 
included in the Rate Year forecast.  Additionally, as mentioned on pages 34 and 35 of our 
testimony, the Company has filled 13.2 incremental FTEs internally as of November 6, 2020 and 
8 of those previous positions have not been backfilled.  As such, this further demonstrates that 
the adjusted Historic Test Year headcount is overstated and contains vacant positions in the Rate 
Year.

Subject: 
Opex Associated with Capex Adjustment 
Question: 
1. The questions below all relate to the SEIOP’s adjustment of incremental opex associated
with capex presented in the Department of Public Service Staff’s (“Staff”) revenue
requirement model as adjustment 4(h)12.  The Company’s forecast of incremental opex
associated with capex included in the opex forecast in Other Initiatives in Exhibit __ (RRP-
3), Schedule 27 is supported by the plant forecast model in the Incremental Opex tab
provided to Staff in Exhibit __ (RRP-11), Workpapers for Exhibit RRP-3, Schedule 27,
Workpaper 1.  The Company’s incremental opex associated with capex calculation (1)
utilizes a three-year average transmission line percentage of 6.32 percent and a three-year
average transmission substation percentage of 0.39 percent and (2) excludes certain capex
projects including land purchases, Grounding and Bonding project and FERC 1000 projects
(Niagara-Packard 193/194, Reconductoring 30 line EHI, and EHI Edic Upgrades –
Substation).
a.
Please confirm that, in SEIOP’s opex associated capex adjustment, the transmission line
percentage of 6.32 percent was applied to both transmission line and transmission
substation capex reductions as well as the capex reductions related to the excluded
projects noted above.
b. Please confirm that Staff’s adjustment 4(h)12 should have been segregated between

Response: 
a) Yes.  The Panel applied 6.3 percent to the entire transmission budget, both transmission

Company mentioned in the question above.

the 0.39 percent to the substation projects.
c) The Panel agrees that the Opex associated with CapEx should reflect the separation of
transmission line and substation projects as well as the capex project exclusions noted
above.  This would result in a smaller downward adjustment to the Transmission Opex as
a whole; a reduction of $4.384 million in the Rate Year, $6.064 million in RY2, and
$6.467 million in RY3.

Subject: 
Transportation 
 
 
Question: 
 
1. In calculating the removal of 982 vehicles from the Company’s forecast of lease expense, 
related to replacement vehicles as discussed in the testimony of the Staff Accounting Panel at 
pages 24 through 35, how did the panel account for the residual lease expense for the 982 
vehicles if they are not replaced?  For example, if the 982 vehicles removed by Staff are not 
replaced, there will still be an associated monthly lease cost for each associated vehicle, 
related to Heavy Vehicle Use Tax, Rental Tax, and Management Fees. 
 
 
Response: 
 
As discussed in the Direct Testimony of the Staff Accounting Panel, the Panel adjusted the 
Company’s Rate Year forecasted Transportation Expense to reflect a reduction to the Company’s 
forecasted level of vehicle replacements from 1,557 vehicle replacements to 575 vehicle 
replacements, or a difference of 982 vehicles.  In order to calculate the incremental costs 
associated with the 982 vehicles, the SAP utilized the information provided by the Company in 
response to IRs DPS-459 and DPS-1053.  The Company did not provide any workpapers or 
schedules in response to these or any other information requests that break down the costs of the 
vehicle lease expense or identify the amount of the leasing costs that are related to other fees.  
Therefore, the Panel’s adjustment does not include any residual costs associated with the 
vehicles that will not be replaced.

Subject: 
Storms 
 
 
Question: 
 
Please explain how the electric inflation shown on the “Minor Storms” line of the Inflation 
Adjustment workpaper as presented on Exhibit___(SAP-2), Page 20 of 27 is not double counted 
as part of the inflation adjustments shown on the other lines in that workpaper, specifically 
Contractors, Consultants, Employee Expenses, Materials, Other Employee Benefits, Other 
Expenses and Transportation. 
 
 
Response: 
 
The inflation adjustment shown on Exhibit___(SAP-2), page 20 of 27, related to  “Minor 
Storms” inadvertently reflects an inflation adjustment for other elements of expense (i.e., 
contractors, consultants, employee expenses, materials, other employee benefits, other expenses 
and transportation costs) in which the inflation adjustment is already reflected for those 
respective cost elements.  As shown in Attachment 1 the inflation adjustment related to “Minor 
Storms” should have only reflected the inflation related to the difference in the CY 2019 minor 
storm costs, adjusted for the proposed new major storm deferral threshold, and the three-year 
average minor storm costs.  This results in a reduction to Staff’s recommended inflation 
adjustment of approximately $0.082M.
